**(Benefit: That divorce is not a prohibition)**

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some preceding discussion:

Evidence that divorce is not a prohibition is that Allah the Exalted permitted it, and He has never permitted the prohibition of what is lawful. Prohibition does not rest with the servant. Rather, what rests with him are the causes, and the making lawful or unlawful follows them. So it is like manumission (*'itq*), exactly the same. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾

Then He prescribed the *tahillah* (the means of dissolving an oath) for the prohibition of what is lawful. The Prophet (ﷺ) divorced Hafsah, and it was not a prohibition of her. Had divorce been a prohibition, expiation would have been prescribed for it, as it was prescribed for prohibiting what is lawful, and as it was prescribed for *zihar*, which is a prohibition.

**[Section: The ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which he explained from his Lord, the Blessed and Exalted, concerning one who prohibits his slave-girl, his wife, or his property]**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths.﴾

It is established in the two *Sahihs* (of Bukhari and Muslim) that he (ﷺ) drank honey in the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, and Aishah and Hafsah conspired against him until he said: "I will not return to it." In another wording: "and she had sworn."

In the *Sunan of al-Nasa'i*, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a slave-girl whom he had intercourse with. Aishah and Hafsah kept at him until he prohibited her, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾"

In *Sahih Muslim*, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "If a man prohibits his wife, it is an oath which he expiates." And he recited: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there is an excellent example for you.﴾

In *Jami' al-Tirmidhi*, from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) swore off from his wives and prohibited, so he made the prohibited lawful, and he made an expiation for the oath." Thus it was narrated by Maslamah ibn Alqamah, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, from Aishah. But Ali ibn Mushir and others narrated it from al-Sha'bi, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a *mursal* (a report missing a companion from its chain), and this is more authentic. End of the words of Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi).

Her saying "he made the prohibited lawful" means that he made lawful the thing he had prohibited, which was the honey or the slave-girl, after his prohibiting it.

Layth ibn Sa'd said, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abdullah ibn Hubayrah, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, who said: "I asked Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them) about one who said to his wife, 'You are prohibited to me (*anti 'alayya haram*),' and they both said: 'It is an expiation of an oath.'"

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said concerning prohibition: "It is an oath which he expiates."

Ibn Hazm said: this was also narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Aishah, Mother of the Believers. Al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal said: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to us, who said: "I asked Nafi', the freedman of Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), about *al-haram*: is it a divorce? He said: 'No. Did not the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibit his slave-girl? Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him to make expiation for his oath, and He did not make her prohibited to him.'"

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, both from Ikrimah, that Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "It is an oath," meaning the prohibition.

Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: al-Muqaddami narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Sakhr ibn Juwayriyyah, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "*Al-haram* is an oath."

In *Sahih al-Bukhari*, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he heard Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) say: "If one prohibits his wife, it is nothing," and he recited: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there is an excellent example for you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]. It was said that this is another narration from Ibn Abbas. It was also said that he meant only that it is not a divorce, and that in it there is an expiation of an oath, and for this reason he cited the act of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This second view is more evident.

On this question there are twenty opinions among people. We will mention them, their aspects, their sources, and the most preponderant among them, with the help and success of Allah the Exalted.

**The first:** That prohibition is idle, with nothing in it, neither concerning the wife nor anyone else. There is no divorce, no *ila'*, no oath, and no *zihar*. Waki' narrated from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq: "I do not care whether I have prohibited my wife or a bowl of *tharid* (bread soaked in broth)."

Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, from al-Thawri, from Salih ibn Muslim, from al-Sha'bi, that he said concerning the prohibition of a woman: "She is less to me than my sandal."

It was mentioned from Ibn Jurayj: Abd al-Karim informed me, from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that he said: "I do not care whether I have prohibited her," meaning his wife, "or prohibited the water of the river."

Qatadah said: A man asked Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Himyari about this, and he said: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you are free, labour, and to your Lord turn with longing﴾ [al-Sharh: 7–8]. "You are a man who plays, so go and play." This is the view of all the people of the literal (*Zahiri*) school.

**The second view:** That prohibition concerning the wife is three divorces. Ibn Hazm said: This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ibn Umar, and it is the view of al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and it was narrated from al-Hakam ibn Utaybah.

I say: What is established from Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umar is what Layth narrated: from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu Hubayrah, from Qabisah, that he asked Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umar about one who said to his wife, "You are prohibited to me," and they both said: "It is an expiation of an oath." Nothing contrary to this is authentically reported from them.

As for Ali, Abu Muhammad (Ibn Hazm) narrated through Yahya al-Qattan, who said: Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "People say concerning *al-haram*: she is prohibited until she marries another husband. By Allah, Ali did not say that. Rather, Ali said: 'I do not make her lawful, nor do I make her prohibited to you. If you wish, go forward, and if you wish, hold back.'"

As for al-Hasan, Abu Muhammad narrated through Qatadah from him that he said: "Everything lawful to me is prohibited, then it is an oath." Perhaps Abu Muhammad made an error regarding Ali, Zayd, and Ibn Umar, confusing them with the matter of *al-khaliyyah* (the one who is "free"), *al-bariyyah* (the one who is "clear"), and *al-battah* (the irrevocable divorce), for Ahmad related from them that these are three divorces.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: What Abu Muhammad reported from Ali and Ibn Umar is authentic, but he was mistaken in attributing it to "You are prohibited to me," which is a clear error. For they distinguished between prohibition, on which they issued fatwas that it is an oath, and *al-khaliyyah*, on which they issued fatwas that it is three. I do not know of anyone who said it is three in every case.

**The third view:** That it is three in the case of a woman who has been consummated, and nothing else is accepted from him. If she has not been consummated, what he intended takes effect: one, two, or three. If he uses it without qualification, it is one. If he says, "I did not intend divorce," then if there was previously a statement that can be applied to it, it is accepted from him; if it was initiated without a prior statement, it is not accepted. If he prohibits his slave-girl, his food, or his property, it is nothing. This is the view of Malik.

**The fourth view:** That if he intended divorce, it is divorce. Then, if he intended three, it is three; if he intended less, it is one irrevocable divorce. If he intended an oath, it is an oath in which there is expiation. If he did not intend anything, it is an *ila'* with the ruling of *ila'*. If he intended a lie, he is believed in the fatwa, and it is nothing; but in judgment it is *ila'*. If it falls on someone other than the wife, such as a slave-girl, food, or otherwise, it is an oath with expiation for it. This is the view of Abu Hanifah.

**The fifth view:** That if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and what he intended takes effect. If he used it without qualification, it is one divorce. If he intended *zihar*, it is *zihar*. If he intended an oath, it is an oath. If he intended the prohibition of her very self without divorce or *zihar*, then he owes an expiation of an oath. If he did not intend anything, then there are two opinions: one, that nothing is binding on him; the other, that he owes an expiation of an oath. If it falls on a slave-girl and he intended her manumission, manumission takes effect. If he intended her prohibition, an expiation of an oath is binding on him by the utterance itself. If he intended *zihar* from her, it is not valid and nothing is binding on him; but it was said that an expiation of an oath is binding on him. If he did not intend anything, then there are two opinions: one, nothing is binding on him; the other, he owes an expiation of an oath. If it falls on someone other than the wife or the slave-girl, it does not become prohibited, and nothing is binding on him by it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

**The sixth view:** That it is *zihar* by its unqualified use, whether he intended it or not, unless he directs it by intention to divorce or oath, in which case it takes the meaning he intended. This is the apparent view of Ahmad.

It is also reported from him in a second narration that by its unqualified use it is an oath, unless he directs it by intention to *zihar* or divorce, in which case it takes the meaning he intended. And there is a third narration from him: that it is *zihar* in every case, even if he intended something else. And there is a fourth narration, related by Abu al-Husayn in his *Furu'*: that it is irrevocable divorce. If he joined it with his saying, "I mean by it divorce," then there are two narrations from him concerning it. One: it is divorce; on this, is it three that is binding, or one? On two narrations. The second: it is also *zihar*, just as if he said, "You are to me like my mother's back; I mean by it divorce." This is the summary of his view.

**The seventh view:** That if he intended three by it, it is three; if he intended one, it is one irrevocable; if he intended an oath, it is an oath; and if he did not intend anything, it is a lie with nothing in it. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, related from him by Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm.

**The eighth view:** That it is one irrevocable divorce in every case. This is the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman.

**The ninth view:** That if he intended three, it is three; and if he intended one, or did not intend anything, it is one irrevocable. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, related from him by Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm.

**The tenth view:** That it is one revocable divorce. This was related by Ibn al-Sabbagh, and his companion Abu Bakr al-Shashi, from al-Zuhri, from Umar ibn al-Khattab.

**The eleventh view:** That she becomes prohibited to him by that alone, and these people did not classify it as *zihar*, nor divorce, nor oath, but instead imposed on him the consequence of its prohibition. Ibn Hazm said: This is authentically reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib and some companions who were not named, and from Abu Hurayrah.

It is also authentically reported from al-Hasan, Khilas ibn Amr, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatadah that they commanded him only to avoid her.

**The twelfth view:** Suspension in this matter, that the mufti neither makes her prohibited to the husband nor makes her lawful to him. This is as al-Sha'bi reported from Ali, that he said: "I do not make her lawful, nor do I make her prohibited to you. If you wish, go forward, and if you wish, hold back."

**The thirteenth view:** The distinction between one who makes the prohibition immediate or conditioned by a deliberate condition, and one who puts it in the form of an oath. The first is *zihar* in every case, even if he intended divorce by it, and even if he joined it with his saying, "I mean by it divorce." The second is an oath requiring an expiation of an oath. So if he says, "You are prohibited to me," or "When Ramadan comes, you are prohibited to me," it is *zihar*. And if he says, "If I travel," or "If I eat this food," or "If I speak to so-and-so, then my wife is prohibited to me," it is an oath with expiation. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.

These are the basic views on this question, and they branch out into more than twenty opinions.

**[Section: The disagreement concerning the prohibition of other than the wife]**

It has become clear from what we have mentioned that whoever prohibits something other than his wife, such as food, drink, clothing, or his slave-girl, does not thereby become prohibited to himself, and he owes an expiation of an oath. On this there is disagreement in three places.

The first: that it is not prohibited. This is the view of the majority. Abu Hanifah said: it is prohibited with a restricted prohibition which expiation removes, just as when one makes *zihar* from his wife: it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until he makes expiation. Also, Allah the Exalted named the expiation in that case a *tahillah*, which is what makes lawful, and this shows that the prohibition existed before it. And also, He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ And also, it is a prohibition of what was permitted to him, so it is prohibited by his prohibiting it, just as if he prohibited his wife.

Those who dispute with him say: The expiation was named a *tahillah* from the "dissolving" (*hall*) which is the opposite of a binding contract, not from the "lawfulness" (*hill*) which is the opposite of prohibition; so it dissolves the oath after its binding.

As for His saying: ﴿Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, what is meant is the prohibition of the slave-girl or the honey, and restraining himself from it; and that is called prohibition. So it is a prohibition by speech, not an establishment of prohibition by the Law.

Ibn al-Qayyim's argument from analogy with the zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likens his wife to his mother), or with his saying "You are unlawful to me" (anti ʿalayya ḥarām), is as follows. If this analogy were sound, expiation would have to come before breaking the oath, just as in zihar, since the ruling would be the same in meaning. According to them, however, expiation is not permitted except after breaking the oath. Their position therefore entails one of two things, and there is no escape from either. Either he does the forbidden act, although Allah has ordained the release of oaths (tahillat al-yamin, the dissolution of oaths), in which case something forbidden would be ordained or would follow from what is ordained, since he cannot reach the release except by doing the thing sworn against. Or he has no way of doing the act lawfully, because expiation may not be advanced so that he could thereby gain permission, and so his doing it, which is forbidden, is impossible. This is what has been said on the question from both sides.

Furthermore, the matter has depth, and it is subtle and obscure. Whoever forbids something is in the position of one who swears by Allah to abandon it. If he swears to abandon it, he may not violate the sanctity of the thing sworn by through doing it, except by undertaking expiation. Once he undertakes it, he may proceed to do what he swore against. But if he resolves not to expiate, the Lawgiver does not permit him to proceed with what he swore against. The Lawgiver grants him permission and makes it lawful only when he undertakes what Allah has ordained of expiation. His permission and the lifting of the prohibition after he refrained from it by oath or by forbidding, is therefore a concession from Allah to him and a favour from Him, because he has undertaken His ruling, which is the expiation He ordained. If he does not undertake it, the prohibition that he imposed upon himself remains a burden on him. Allah lifts burdens only from those who fear Him and undertake His ruling. In the law before us, an oath was binding, its fulfilment was mandatory, and breaking it was not permitted. Allah eased this for this community and permitted it to break oaths on condition of expiation. So if one does not expiate, either before or after, no concession is granted to him to break the oath. This is the meaning of the statement that it is forbidden until he expiates.

This is not a peculiarity of Abu Hanifa. It is one of the two opinions in the school of Ahmad. This is clarified by the fact that this forbidding and this oath involve two prohibitions: a prohibition he places upon himself regarding the act, and a prohibition from the Lawgiver against breaking the oath without expiation. If the forbidding and the oath did not make it forbidden, then his self-prohibition would have no effect, and neither would the Lawgiver's prohibition. The most that would follow is that the Lawgiver obliged him, because of this prohibition, to give charity, free a slave, or fast, and none of these would affect whether the sworn-against thing becomes lawful or remains forbidden. It would be equal before and after the prohibition, so expiation would have no effect at all, neither in prohibiting nor in permitting. The corruption of this is not hidden.

As for the objection that he is obliged to do it while it is forbidden, since advancing the expiation is not permitted, the answer is that he is permitted to proceed only when he resolves to expiate. His resolve to expiate removes the continuation of the prohibition for him. The prohibition remains only if he does not undertake the expiation. When he undertakes it, the prohibition does not continue.

[Section: The expiation for forbidding]

The second position is that the forbidding obliges him to expiate, and that it is like an oath. This is the view of the Companions we have named, and the view of the jurists of opinion and of hadith, except al-Shafiʿi and Malik, who said there is no expiation for it.

Those who required expiation have better support from the text than those who dropped it. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the release of oaths right after His words: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1]. This is explicit that the forbidding of what is lawful has had the release of oaths ordained for it, either specifically or as something that includes it and other things. It is not permitted to separate the cause of the expiation mentioned in the context from the ruling of expiation and attach it to something else. This is clearly impossible.

Also, the prohibition of an act by forbidding is like the prohibition of it by oath, and even stronger. If an oath involves violating the sanctity of His name, then forbidding involves violating the sanctity of His law and command. When He legislates something as lawful and a person forbids it, his forbidding is a violation of the sanctity of what He legislated. We say that breaking an oath does not involve violating the sanctity of the Name, nor does forbidding involve violating the sanctity of the Law, as some jurists say. This is a very corrupt reasoning. Breaking an oath is either permissible, obligatory, or recommended. Allah has never permitted anyone to violate the sanctity of His name, yet He legislated for His servants breaking oaths together with expiation. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that:

"Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him expiate for his oath and do the thing he swore against."

It is known that violating the sanctity of His name, blessed and exalted is He, has never been permitted in any law. Expiation is, as Allah named it, a tahillah (release), which is a form (tafʿilah) from the root "to untie." It releases what the oath bound. This binding happens by oath and also by forbidding. The secret of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the release of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2], after His words: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, becomes clear.

[Section: Swearing by divorce and by "the unlawful" has two forms]

It is known that swearing by divorce has two forms. One is: "If I do such and such, then you are divorced." The second is: "Divorce is binding on me that I will not do such and such." The disagreement over these two forms has existed from ancient times until now. Likewise, swearing by "the unlawful" has two forms. One is: "If I do such and such, then you are unlawful to me," or "What Allah has made lawful is unlawful to me." The second is: "The unlawful is binding on me that I will not do such and such."

Whoever says regarding "divorce is binding on me" that it is neither explicit nor implicit, and nothing takes effect by it, then regarding "the unlawful is binding on me" it is even more so. Whoever says it is implicit, then if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and otherwise not. Likewise, regarding "the unlawful is binding on me," if he intended forbidding by it, it is as if he intended divorce by saying "divorce." He has thereby bound himself to forbid, just as he bound himself to divorce. This is a binding of forbidding, and that is a binding of divorce. If he intended by it "what Allah has forbidden to me, its forbidding is binding on me," it is neither an oath, nor a forbidding, nor a divorce, nor a zihar. It is not permitted to separate a Muslim from his wife by a word that was not established for divorce and that he did not intend. He is obliged to the expiation of an oath of prohibition, because of the strength of the oath. It is not like swearing by a created thing, which is not binding and is not even a vain oath. This is a valid binding oath, so it carries the expiation of an oath.

Ibn Abbas gave this fatwa, and he traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is authentically transmitted from him, by the most authentic chain: "The unlawful is an oath which he expiates." Then he said: ﴿Indeed you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21].

This is also the ruling for his saying: "If I do such and such, then you are unlawful to me." This is more fitting for the expiation of an oath than his saying: "You are unlawful to me."

Regarding "You are unlawful to me," or "What Allah has made lawful is unlawful to me," or "You are unlawful to me like carrion, blood, or the flesh of swine," there are several positions:

The first: it is vain and void, and nothing follows from it. This is one of the two reports from Ibn Abbas. Masruq, Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, Ata, al-Sha'bi, Dawud, all the people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir), and most of the people of hadith held this. It is also one of the two views of the Malikis, chosen by Asbagh ibn al-Faraj.

In the Sahih, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he heard Ibn Abbas say: "If he forbids his wife, it is nothing. Indeed you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example." It is authentically transmitted from Masruq that he said: "I do not care whether I forbid my wife or a bowl of stew." It is authentically transmitted from al-Sha'bi regarding forbidding a woman: "It is less significant to me than my sandal."

Abu Salamah said: "I do not care whether I forbid my wife or forbid the water of the river."

Al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal said: A man made his wife unlawful to himself, and asked Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman about it. Humayd said to him: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when you are free, then labour, and to your Lord turn with eagerness﴾ [al-Sharh: 7–8]. You are a man who plays; so go and play.

The second position: it is three divorces. This is the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. The Commander of the Faithful Ali judged with three divorces concerning Adi ibn Qays al-Kilabi, and said to him: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you touch her before she marries someone other than you, I will surely stone you." The argument for this view is that she is not made unlawful to him except by three divorces, so the occurrence of three divorces follows necessarily from her being unlawful to him.

The third position: by this statement she becomes unlawful to him, without any mention of divorce. This is also authentically transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, Khilas ibn Amr, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatadah. These did not mention divorce, but only ordered him to abstain from her.

This is also authentically transmitted from Ali, peace be upon him. Either there are two reports from him, or he intended the forbidding of three. The argument for this view is that his statement only implied forbidding and did not address the number of divorces, so she became unlawful to him by the implication of his forbidding.

The fourth position: suspension regarding it. This is authentically transmitted from the Commander of the Faithful Ali as well, and it is the view of al-Sha'bi. He said: "Some men say regarding 'the lawful is unlawful' that she is unlawful until she marries another husband, and they attribute this to Ali. By Allah, Ali did not say that. He only said: 'I am neither making her lawful for you nor making her unlawful for you. If you wish, go forward, and if you wish, hold back.'" The argument of these is that forbidding is not divorce, and he does not possess the power to forbid what is lawful. He only possesses the power to create the cause by which he forbids, which is divorce. This is not explicit in divorce, and it is not something for which the custom of the Law has been established regarding forbidding a wife, so the matter is unclear.

The fifth position: if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce; otherwise it is an oath. This is the view of Tawus, al-Zuhri, al-Shafiʿi, and a report from al-Hasan. The argument for this view is that it is implicit in divorce. If he intended it, it is divorce; if he did not intend it, it is an oath, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ up to His words: ﴿the release of your oaths﴾.

The sixth position: if he intended three by it, it is three; if he intended one, it is one irrevocable divorce; if he intended an oath, it is an oath; and if he intended nothing, it is a lie with nothing in it. This was said by Sufyan, and al-Nakha'i related it from his companions. The argument for this view is that the wording allows for what he intended of these, so he follows his intention.

The seventh position: like this, except that if he intended nothing, it is an oath that he expiates. This is the view of al-Awza'i. The argument for this view is the apparent meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the release of your oaths﴾.

If he intended divorce by it, it is not an oath. If he divorced and did not intend divorce, it is an oath.

The eighth position: likewise, except that if he intended nothing, it is one irrevocable divorce, in application of the wording of forbidding.

The ninth position: that it carries the expiation of zihar. This is authentically transmitted from Ibn Abbas as well, and from Abu Qilabah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and Uthman al-Taymi. It is one of the reports from Imam Ahmad. The argument for this view is that Allah, exalted is He, made likening a woman to his mother, who is forbidden to him, a zihar, and called it a repugnant word and a falsehood. If likening her to a forbidden woman makes him a person who has done zihar, then when he explicitly declares her forbidden, it is even more fitting that it be zihar.

This is the most sound and well-grounded of the opinions, and it is supported by the fact that Allah did not grant the legally responsible person (al-mukallaf) the authority to make something forbidden (tahrim) or permissible (tahlil). That authority belongs to Allah the Exalted alone. He granted the servant only the actions and statements that bring about forbiddance or permissibility. So the cause (al-sabab) rests with the servant, and the ruling (hukm) rests with Allah the Exalted. If a man says, "You are to me like my mother's back" (anti 'alayya ka-zahri ummi), or says, "You are forbidden to me" (anti 'alayya haram), he has uttered an objectionable and false statement (al-munkar min al-qawl wa al-zur), and he has lied. Allah did not make her like his mother's back, nor did He make her forbidden to him. Yet by this statement, with its objectionable falsehood, He has obligated him to the more severe of the two expiations, which is the expiation of zihar (kaffarat al-zihar, a formal expiation for comparing one's wife to one's mother).

The tenth opinion: it is a single revocable divorce (talaqah wahidah). This is one of the two reports from Umar ibn al-Khattab, and it is the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, the teacher of Abu Hanifa. The proof for this view is that a divorce by prohibition (talaq al-tahrim) does not necessarily imply a triple prohibition. It is satisfied by the least of it, and a single divorce is certain. So the wording is taken to mean that, because it is the certain meaning. This is analogous to prohibition by the completion of the waiting period ('iddah).

The eleventh opinion: he is held to what he intended by it regarding the basic fact of divorce and its number. If he intended prohibition without divorce, then it is an expiable oath (yamin mukaffirah). This is the view of al-Shafi'i. The proof for this view is that the wording is capable of all of these meanings, so none of them is fixed except by intention. If he intended mere prohibition, then it is a refusal to have her by means of prohibition, just as refusal by oath is, and she is not forbidden to him in either of the two cases.

The twelfth opinion: he is also held to his intention regarding the basic fact of divorce and its number. However, if he intended one divorce, it is a final irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in). If he did not intend divorce at all, then he is a mu'li (one who has made an oath of abstention, ila'). If he intended a lie, then it has no effect. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. The proof for this view is that the wording admits of what has been mentioned. However, if he intended one divorce, it is irrevocable, because prohibition implies irrevocable separation (al-bayunah), which is of two kinds, minor (sughra) and major (kubra). The minor is the one that is definitely established, so it is taken into account rather than the major. There is another report from him: if he intended a lie, he is believed in matters between himself and Allah but is not accepted in legal judgment. Rather, he is a mu'li and not a zahir, according to him, whether he intended it or not. And if he explicitly said, "I mean by it zihar," he is not a zahir.

The thirteenth opinion: it is an oath, and what expiates an oath expiates it in every case. This was also reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas, Aisha, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud, Abdullah ibn Umar, Ikrimah, Ata, Makhul, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Nafi', al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and others besides them. The proof for this view is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted mentioned the obligation of the dissolution of oaths (tahillat al-ayman) immediately after the prohibition of what is lawful. So it must certainly include this case. It is not permissible to make the dissolution of oaths apply to something other than what was mentioned before it, and the thing mentioned is removed from the ruling of dissolution, for which its mention was intended.

The fourteenth opinion: it is an aggravated oath (yamin mughallazah), in which the freeing of a slave (itq raqabah) is specifically required. This was also reported from Ibn Abbas, Abu Bakr, Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and a group of the Successors (al-tabi'un). The proof for this view is that, since it is an aggravated oath, its expiation is made more severe by the requirement of freeing a slave with no alternative. The reason for its severity is that it includes the prohibition of what Allah has made lawful, which is not up to the servant. As for the statement of objectionable falsehood, if he intended it as a report, then it is a lie in his report and transgressive in his oath. So its expiation is made severe by the requirement of freeing a slave, just as the expiation of zihar is made severe by it, or by fasting two consecutive months, or by feeding sixty of the poor.

The fifteenth opinion: it is a divorce. Then, if she was not consummated, it is what he intended, a single divorce or more. If she was consummated, it is three divorces, even if he intended less. This is one of the two reports from Malik. The proof for this view is that since the wording implies prohibition, its ruling must follow from it. A woman who has not been consummated is forbidden by one divorce, while a woman who has been consummated is not forbidden except by three.

[The positions of the Malikis on the question]
After this, there are five opinions in the school of Malik. This one is the best known. The second is that it is three divorces in every case, whether he intended three or not. Abd al-Malik chose this in his al-Mabsut. The third is that it is a single irrevocable divorce absolutely. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad related this as a report from Malik. The fourth is that it is a single revocable divorce. This is the view of Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Salamah. The fifth is that it is whatever he intended of that, absolutely, whether before consummation or after. You already know the justification for these opinions.

[The position of the Shafi'i school on the question]
As for the precise statement of the school of al-Shafi'i: if he intended zihar by it, it is zihar. If he intended prohibition by it, it is a prohibition which entails nothing except the obligation of expiation. If he intended divorce, it is divorce, and it is what he intended. If he stated it without specifying intention, his companions have three positions. The first is that it is explicit (sarih) in requiring expiation. The second is that nothing follows from it. The third is that for a slave-woman it is explicit in prohibition, which requires expiation, while for a free woman it is an allusion (kinayah). They said: the original verse was revealed concerning a slave-woman. They said: if a man says, "You are forbidden to me," and then says, "I intended by it zihar and divorce," Ibn al-Haddad said: he is told, "Specify one of the two matters, because a single word cannot be both zihar and divorce at once." It was also said: he is bound by whichever of the two he began with. They said: if a man claims a right against another man, and he denies it, and the claimant says, "The lawful is forbidden to you, the intention is my intention, not yours, I have nothing against you," and the other says, "The lawful is forbidden to me, and the intention in that is your intention, you have nothing from me," then the intention is the intention of the one swearing, not the one who makes him swear, because intention can only come from the one who has the authority to effect the ruling.

[Section: The position of Imam Ahmad on the question]
As for the precise statement of the position of Imam Ahmad: it is zihar in its very wording, even if he did not intend it, unless he intends divorce or oath by it, in which case he is held to what he intended. There is a second report from him that it is an oath in its very wording, unless he intends divorce or zihar by it, in which case he is held to what he intended. There is a third report from him that it is zihar in every case. If he intended divorce or oath by it, it is neither an oath nor a divorce, just as if he intended divorce or oath by saying, "You are to me like my mother's back," since both wordings are explicit in zihar. According to this third report, if he connects it with "I mean by it divorce," then is it divorce or zihar? There are two reports. The first is that it is zihar, just as if he said, "You are to me like my mother's back, I mean by it divorce or prohibition," since prohibition is explicit in zihar. The second is that it is divorce, because he has explicitly stated his intention with a word that admits of it, and at most it is an allusion in it. According to this report, if he says, "I mean by it one divorce," she is divorced once. If he says, "I mean by it the divorce," then is she divorced three times or once? There are two reports, whose basis is whether the obligation is taken as the genus or as the general. This is the precise statement and exposition of his position.

[The position of Ibn Taymiyyah on the question]
In this question there is another position beyond all of these, which is that if he pronounces prohibition, it is zihar even if he intended divorce by it. If he swears by it, it is an expiable oath. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and both the text and analogy indicate it. When he pronounces it, he has uttered an objectionable statement and falsehood, and he is more deserving of the expiation of zihar than one who compares his wife to a forbidden woman. When he swears by it, it is an oath among oaths, just as if he swore by pledging to free a slave, to perform the pilgrimage, or to give charity. This is pure analogy and understanding. Do you not see that if he says, "For Allah, I must free a slave, or perform the pilgrimage, or fast," it becomes binding on him? And if he says, "If I speak to so-and-so, then it is for Allah binding on me to do that," as an oath, it is an oath. Likewise, if he says, "He is a Jew or a Christian," he has disbelieved by that. And if he says, "If I do such-and-such, then he is a Jew or a Christian," it is an oath. The consistent extension of this, indeed its exact counterpart in every respect, is that if he says, "You are to me like my mother's back," it is zihar. So if he says, "If I do such-and-such, then you are to me like my mother's back," it is an oath. The consistent extension of this also is that if he says, "You are divorced," it is divorce, and if he says, "If I do such-and-such, then you are divorced," it is his oath. These are the sound principles, consistently applied, drawn from the Book, the Sunnah, and the balance of reason. And success is from Allah.

**(Benefit: That divorce is not a prohibition)**

Ibn al-Qayyim said, after some preceding discussion:

Evidence that divorce is not a prohibition is that Allah the Exalted permitted it, and He has never permitted the prohibition of what is lawful. Prohibition does not rest with the servant. Rather, what rests with him are the causes, and the making lawful or unlawful follows them. So it is like manumission (*'itq*), exactly the same. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾

Then He prescribed the *tahillah* (the means of dissolving an oath) for the prohibition of what is lawful. The Prophet (ﷺ) divorced Hafsah, and it was not a prohibition of her. Had divorce been a prohibition, expiation would have been prescribed for it, as it was prescribed for prohibiting what is lawful, and as it was prescribed for *zihar*, which is a prohibition.

**[Section: The ruling of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which he explained from his Lord, the Blessed and Exalted, concerning one who prohibits his slave-girl, his wife, or his property]**

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful. Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths.﴾

It is established in the two *Sahihs* (of Bukhari and Muslim) that he (ﷺ) drank honey in the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, and Aishah and Hafsah conspired against him until he said: "I will not return to it." In another wording: "and she had sworn."

In the *Sunan of al-Nasa'i*, from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him): "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had a slave-girl whom he had intercourse with. Aishah and Hafsah kept at him until he prohibited her, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾"

In *Sahih Muslim*, from Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "If a man prohibits his wife, it is an oath which he expiates." And he recited: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there is an excellent example for you.﴾

In *Jami' al-Tirmidhi*, from Aishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) swore off from his wives and prohibited, so he made the prohibited lawful, and he made an expiation for the oath." Thus it was narrated by Maslamah ibn Alqamah, from Dawud, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, from Aishah. But Ali ibn Mushir and others narrated it from al-Sha'bi, from the Prophet (ﷺ), as a *mursal* (a report missing a companion from its chain), and this is more authentic. End of the words of Abu Isa (al-Tirmidhi).

Her saying "he made the prohibited lawful" means that he made lawful the thing he had prohibited, which was the honey or the slave-girl, after his prohibiting it.

Layth ibn Sa'd said, from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abdullah ibn Hubayrah, from Qabisah ibn Dhu'ayb, who said: "I asked Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them) about one who said to his wife, 'You are prohibited to me (*anti 'alayya haram*),' and they both said: 'It is an expiation of an oath.'"

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ibn Uyaynah, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him), who said concerning prohibition: "It is an oath which he expiates."

Ibn Hazm said: this was also narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Aishah, Mother of the Believers. Al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal said: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to us, who said: "I asked Nafi', the freedman of Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), about *al-haram*: is it a divorce? He said: 'No. Did not the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prohibit his slave-girl? Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded him to make expiation for his oath, and He did not make her prohibited to him.'"

Abd al-Razzaq said, from Ma'mar, from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani, both from Ikrimah, that Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "It is an oath," meaning the prohibition.

Isma'il ibn Ishaq said: al-Muqaddami narrated to us, Hammad ibn Zayd narrated to us, from Sakhr ibn Juwayriyyah, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), who said: "*Al-haram* is an oath."

In *Sahih al-Bukhari*, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he heard Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) say: "If one prohibits his wife, it is nothing," and he recited: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah there is an excellent example for you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21]. It was said that this is another narration from Ibn Abbas. It was also said that he meant only that it is not a divorce, and that in it there is an expiation of an oath, and for this reason he cited the act of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). This second view is more evident.

On this question there are twenty opinions among people. We will mention them, their aspects, their sources, and the most preponderant among them, with the help and success of Allah the Exalted.

**The first:** That prohibition is idle, with nothing in it, neither concerning the wife nor anyone else. There is no divorce, no *ila'*, no oath, and no *zihar*. Waki' narrated from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq: "I do not care whether I have prohibited my wife or a bowl of *tharid* (bread soaked in broth)."

Abd al-Razzaq mentioned, from al-Thawri, from Salih ibn Muslim, from al-Sha'bi, that he said concerning the prohibition of a woman: "She is less to me than my sandal."

It was mentioned from Ibn Jurayj: Abd al-Karim informed me, from Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, that he said: "I do not care whether I have prohibited her," meaning his wife, "or prohibited the water of the river."

Qatadah said: A man asked Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Himyari about this, and he said: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿So when you are free, labour, and to your Lord turn with longing﴾ [al-Sharh: 7–8]. "You are a man who plays, so go and play." This is the view of all the people of the literal (*Zahiri*) school.

**The second view:** That prohibition concerning the wife is three divorces. Ibn Hazm said: This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib, Zayd ibn Thabit, and Ibn Umar, and it is the view of al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla, and it was narrated from al-Hakam ibn Utaybah.

I say: What is established from Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umar is what Layth narrated: from Yazid ibn Abi Habib, from Abu Hubayrah, from Qabisah, that he asked Zayd ibn Thabit and Ibn Umar about one who said to his wife, "You are prohibited to me," and they both said: "It is an expiation of an oath." Nothing contrary to this is authentically reported from them.

As for Ali, Abu Muhammad (Ibn Hazm) narrated through Yahya al-Qattan, who said: Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid narrated to us, from al-Sha'bi, who said: "People say concerning *al-haram*: she is prohibited until she marries another husband. By Allah, Ali did not say that. Rather, Ali said: 'I do not make her lawful, nor do I make her prohibited to you. If you wish, go forward, and if you wish, hold back.'"

As for al-Hasan, Abu Muhammad narrated through Qatadah from him that he said: "Everything lawful to me is prohibited, then it is an oath." Perhaps Abu Muhammad made an error regarding Ali, Zayd, and Ibn Umar, confusing them with the matter of *al-khaliyyah* (the one who is "free"), *al-bariyyah* (the one who is "clear"), and *al-battah* (the irrevocable divorce), for Ahmad related from them that these are three divorces.

Ibn al-Qayyim said: What Abu Muhammad reported from Ali and Ibn Umar is authentic, but he was mistaken in attributing it to "You are prohibited to me," which is a clear error. For they distinguished between prohibition, on which they issued fatwas that it is an oath, and *al-khaliyyah*, on which they issued fatwas that it is three. I do not know of anyone who said it is three in every case.

**The third view:** That it is three in the case of a woman who has been consummated, and nothing else is accepted from him. If she has not been consummated, what he intended takes effect: one, two, or three. If he uses it without qualification, it is one. If he says, "I did not intend divorce," then if there was previously a statement that can be applied to it, it is accepted from him; if it was initiated without a prior statement, it is not accepted. If he prohibits his slave-girl, his food, or his property, it is nothing. This is the view of Malik.

**The fourth view:** That if he intended divorce, it is divorce. Then, if he intended three, it is three; if he intended less, it is one irrevocable divorce. If he intended an oath, it is an oath in which there is expiation. If he did not intend anything, it is an *ila'* with the ruling of *ila'*. If he intended a lie, he is believed in the fatwa, and it is nothing; but in judgment it is *ila'*. If it falls on someone other than the wife, such as a slave-girl, food, or otherwise, it is an oath with expiation for it. This is the view of Abu Hanifah.

**The fifth view:** That if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and what he intended takes effect. If he used it without qualification, it is one divorce. If he intended *zihar*, it is *zihar*. If he intended an oath, it is an oath. If he intended the prohibition of her very self without divorce or *zihar*, then he owes an expiation of an oath. If he did not intend anything, then there are two opinions: one, that nothing is binding on him; the other, that he owes an expiation of an oath. If it falls on a slave-girl and he intended her manumission, manumission takes effect. If he intended her prohibition, an expiation of an oath is binding on him by the utterance itself. If he intended *zihar* from her, it is not valid and nothing is binding on him; but it was said that an expiation of an oath is binding on him. If he did not intend anything, then there are two opinions: one, nothing is binding on him; the other, he owes an expiation of an oath. If it falls on someone other than the wife or the slave-girl, it does not become prohibited, and nothing is binding on him by it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i.

**The sixth view:** That it is *zihar* by its unqualified use, whether he intended it or not, unless he directs it by intention to divorce or oath, in which case it takes the meaning he intended. This is the apparent view of Ahmad.

It is also reported from him in a second narration that by its unqualified use it is an oath, unless he directs it by intention to *zihar* or divorce, in which case it takes the meaning he intended. And there is a third narration from him: that it is *zihar* in every case, even if he intended something else. And there is a fourth narration, related by Abu al-Husayn in his *Furu'*: that it is irrevocable divorce. If he joined it with his saying, "I mean by it divorce," then there are two narrations from him concerning it. One: it is divorce; on this, is it three that is binding, or one? On two narrations. The second: it is also *zihar*, just as if he said, "You are to me like my mother's back; I mean by it divorce." This is the summary of his view.

**The seventh view:** That if he intended three by it, it is three; if he intended one, it is one irrevocable; if he intended an oath, it is an oath; and if he did not intend anything, it is a lie with nothing in it. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri, related from him by Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm.

**The eighth view:** That it is one irrevocable divorce in every case. This is the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman.

**The ninth view:** That if he intended three, it is three; and if he intended one, or did not intend anything, it is one irrevocable. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, related from him by Abu Muhammad Ibn Hazm.

**The tenth view:** That it is one revocable divorce. This was related by Ibn al-Sabbagh, and his companion Abu Bakr al-Shashi, from al-Zuhri, from Umar ibn al-Khattab.

**The eleventh view:** That she becomes prohibited to him by that alone, and these people did not classify it as *zihar*, nor divorce, nor oath, but instead imposed on him the consequence of its prohibition. Ibn Hazm said: This is authentically reported from Ali ibn Abi Talib and some companions who were not named, and from Abu Hurayrah.

It is also authentically reported from al-Hasan, Khilas ibn Amr, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatadah that they commanded him only to avoid her.

**The twelfth view:** Suspension in this matter, that the mufti neither makes her prohibited to the husband nor makes her lawful to him. This is as al-Sha'bi reported from Ali, that he said: "I do not make her lawful, nor do I make her prohibited to you. If you wish, go forward, and if you wish, hold back."

**The thirteenth view:** The distinction between one who makes the prohibition immediate or conditioned by a deliberate condition, and one who puts it in the form of an oath. The first is *zihar* in every case, even if he intended divorce by it, and even if he joined it with his saying, "I mean by it divorce." The second is an oath requiring an expiation of an oath. So if he says, "You are prohibited to me," or "When Ramadan comes, you are prohibited to me," it is *zihar*. And if he says, "If I travel," or "If I eat this food," or "If I speak to so-and-so, then my wife is prohibited to me," it is an oath with expiation. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah.

These are the basic views on this question, and they branch out into more than twenty opinions.

**[Section: The disagreement concerning the prohibition of other than the wife]**

It has become clear from what we have mentioned that whoever prohibits something other than his wife, such as food, drink, clothing, or his slave-girl, does not thereby become prohibited to himself, and he owes an expiation of an oath. On this there is disagreement in three places.

The first: that it is not prohibited. This is the view of the majority. Abu Hanifah said: it is prohibited with a restricted prohibition which expiation removes, just as when one makes *zihar* from his wife: it is not lawful for him to have intercourse with her until he makes expiation. Also, Allah the Exalted named the expiation in that case a *tahillah*, which is what makes lawful, and this shows that the prohibition existed before it. And also, He said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ And also, it is a prohibition of what was permitted to him, so it is prohibited by his prohibiting it, just as if he prohibited his wife.

Those who dispute with him say: The expiation was named a *tahillah* from the "dissolving" (*hall*) which is the opposite of a binding contract, not from the "lawfulness" (*hill*) which is the opposite of prohibition; so it dissolves the oath after its binding.

As for His saying: ﴿Why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, what is meant is the prohibition of the slave-girl or the honey, and restraining himself from it; and that is called prohibition. So it is a prohibition by speech, not an establishment of prohibition by the Law.

Ibn al-Qayyim's argument from analogy with the zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce in which a husband likens his wife to his mother), or with his saying "You are unlawful to me" (anti ʿalayya ḥarām), is as follows. If this analogy were sound, expiation would have to come before breaking the oath, just as in zihar, since the ruling would be the same in meaning. According to them, however, expiation is not permitted except after breaking the oath. Their position therefore entails one of two things, and there is no escape from either. Either he does the forbidden act, although Allah has ordained the release of oaths (tahillat al-yamin, the dissolution of oaths), in which case something forbidden would be ordained or would follow from what is ordained, since he cannot reach the release except by doing the thing sworn against. Or he has no way of doing the act lawfully, because expiation may not be advanced so that he could thereby gain permission, and so his doing it, which is forbidden, is impossible. This is what has been said on the question from both sides.

Furthermore, the matter has depth, and it is subtle and obscure. Whoever forbids something is in the position of one who swears by Allah to abandon it. If he swears to abandon it, he may not violate the sanctity of the thing sworn by through doing it, except by undertaking expiation. Once he undertakes it, he may proceed to do what he swore against. But if he resolves not to expiate, the Lawgiver does not permit him to proceed with what he swore against. The Lawgiver grants him permission and makes it lawful only when he undertakes what Allah has ordained of expiation. His permission and the lifting of the prohibition after he refrained from it by oath or by forbidding, is therefore a concession from Allah to him and a favour from Him, because he has undertaken His ruling, which is the expiation He ordained. If he does not undertake it, the prohibition that he imposed upon himself remains a burden on him. Allah lifts burdens only from those who fear Him and undertake His ruling. In the law before us, an oath was binding, its fulfilment was mandatory, and breaking it was not permitted. Allah eased this for this community and permitted it to break oaths on condition of expiation. So if one does not expiate, either before or after, no concession is granted to him to break the oath. This is the meaning of the statement that it is forbidden until he expiates.

This is not a peculiarity of Abu Hanifa. It is one of the two opinions in the school of Ahmad. This is clarified by the fact that this forbidding and this oath involve two prohibitions: a prohibition he places upon himself regarding the act, and a prohibition from the Lawgiver against breaking the oath without expiation. If the forbidding and the oath did not make it forbidden, then his self-prohibition would have no effect, and neither would the Lawgiver's prohibition. The most that would follow is that the Lawgiver obliged him, because of this prohibition, to give charity, free a slave, or fast, and none of these would affect whether the sworn-against thing becomes lawful or remains forbidden. It would be equal before and after the prohibition, so expiation would have no effect at all, neither in prohibiting nor in permitting. The corruption of this is not hidden.

As for the objection that he is obliged to do it while it is forbidden, since advancing the expiation is not permitted, the answer is that he is permitted to proceed only when he resolves to expiate. His resolve to expiate removes the continuation of the prohibition for him. The prohibition remains only if he does not undertake the expiation. When he undertakes it, the prohibition does not continue.

[Section: The expiation for forbidding]

The second position is that the forbidding obliges him to expiate, and that it is like an oath. This is the view of the Companions we have named, and the view of the jurists of opinion and of hadith, except al-Shafiʿi and Malik, who said there is no expiation for it.

Those who required expiation have better support from the text than those who dropped it. Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the release of oaths right after His words: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ [al-Tahrim: 1]. This is explicit that the forbidding of what is lawful has had the release of oaths ordained for it, either specifically or as something that includes it and other things. It is not permitted to separate the cause of the expiation mentioned in the context from the ruling of expiation and attach it to something else. This is clearly impossible.

Also, the prohibition of an act by forbidding is like the prohibition of it by oath, and even stronger. If an oath involves violating the sanctity of His name, then forbidding involves violating the sanctity of His law and command. When He legislates something as lawful and a person forbids it, his forbidding is a violation of the sanctity of what He legislated. We say that breaking an oath does not involve violating the sanctity of the Name, nor does forbidding involve violating the sanctity of the Law, as some jurists say. This is a very corrupt reasoning. Breaking an oath is either permissible, obligatory, or recommended. Allah has never permitted anyone to violate the sanctity of His name, yet He legislated for His servants breaking oaths together with expiation. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed us that:

"Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better than it, let him expiate for his oath and do the thing he swore against."

It is known that violating the sanctity of His name, blessed and exalted is He, has never been permitted in any law. Expiation is, as Allah named it, a tahillah (release), which is a form (tafʿilah) from the root "to untie." It releases what the oath bound. This binding happens by oath and also by forbidding. The secret of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the release of your oaths﴾ [al-Tahrim: 2], after His words: ﴿Why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾, becomes clear.

[Section: Swearing by divorce and by "the unlawful" has two forms]

It is known that swearing by divorce has two forms. One is: "If I do such and such, then you are divorced." The second is: "Divorce is binding on me that I will not do such and such." The disagreement over these two forms has existed from ancient times until now. Likewise, swearing by "the unlawful" has two forms. One is: "If I do such and such, then you are unlawful to me," or "What Allah has made lawful is unlawful to me." The second is: "The unlawful is binding on me that I will not do such and such."

Whoever says regarding "divorce is binding on me" that it is neither explicit nor implicit, and nothing takes effect by it, then regarding "the unlawful is binding on me" it is even more so. Whoever says it is implicit, then if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce, and otherwise not. Likewise, regarding "the unlawful is binding on me," if he intended forbidding by it, it is as if he intended divorce by saying "divorce." He has thereby bound himself to forbid, just as he bound himself to divorce. This is a binding of forbidding, and that is a binding of divorce. If he intended by it "what Allah has forbidden to me, its forbidding is binding on me," it is neither an oath, nor a forbidding, nor a divorce, nor a zihar. It is not permitted to separate a Muslim from his wife by a word that was not established for divorce and that he did not intend. He is obliged to the expiation of an oath of prohibition, because of the strength of the oath. It is not like swearing by a created thing, which is not binding and is not even a vain oath. This is a valid binding oath, so it carries the expiation of an oath.

Ibn Abbas gave this fatwa, and he traced it to the Prophet (ﷺ). It is authentically transmitted from him, by the most authentic chain: "The unlawful is an oath which he expiates." Then he said: ﴿Indeed you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example﴾ [al-Ahzab: 21].

This is also the ruling for his saying: "If I do such and such, then you are unlawful to me." This is more fitting for the expiation of an oath than his saying: "You are unlawful to me."

Regarding "You are unlawful to me," or "What Allah has made lawful is unlawful to me," or "You are unlawful to me like carrion, blood, or the flesh of swine," there are several positions:

The first: it is vain and void, and nothing follows from it. This is one of the two reports from Ibn Abbas. Masruq, Abu Salamah ibn Abd al-Rahman, Ata, al-Sha'bi, Dawud, all the people of the outward meaning (Ahl al-Zahir), and most of the people of hadith held this. It is also one of the two views of the Malikis, chosen by Asbagh ibn al-Faraj.

In the Sahih, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he heard Ibn Abbas say: "If he forbids his wife, it is nothing. Indeed you have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example." It is authentically transmitted from Masruq that he said: "I do not care whether I forbid my wife or a bowl of stew." It is authentically transmitted from al-Sha'bi regarding forbidding a woman: "It is less significant to me than my sandal."

Abu Salamah said: "I do not care whether I forbid my wife or forbid the water of the river."

Al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal said: A man made his wife unlawful to himself, and asked Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman about it. Humayd said to him: Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So when you are free, then labour, and to your Lord turn with eagerness﴾ [al-Sharh: 7–8]. You are a man who plays; so go and play.

The second position: it is three divorces. This is the view of Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Umar, al-Hasan al-Basri, and Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Layla. The Commander of the Faithful Ali judged with three divorces concerning Adi ibn Qays al-Kilabi, and said to him: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you touch her before she marries someone other than you, I will surely stone you." The argument for this view is that she is not made unlawful to him except by three divorces, so the occurrence of three divorces follows necessarily from her being unlawful to him.

The third position: by this statement she becomes unlawful to him, without any mention of divorce. This is also authentically transmitted from Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, Khilas ibn Amr, Jabir ibn Zayd, and Qatadah. These did not mention divorce, but only ordered him to abstain from her.

This is also authentically transmitted from Ali, peace be upon him. Either there are two reports from him, or he intended the forbidding of three. The argument for this view is that his statement only implied forbidding and did not address the number of divorces, so she became unlawful to him by the implication of his forbidding.

The fourth position: suspension regarding it. This is authentically transmitted from the Commander of the Faithful Ali as well, and it is the view of al-Sha'bi. He said: "Some men say regarding 'the lawful is unlawful' that she is unlawful until she marries another husband, and they attribute this to Ali. By Allah, Ali did not say that. He only said: 'I am neither making her lawful for you nor making her unlawful for you. If you wish, go forward, and if you wish, hold back.'" The argument of these is that forbidding is not divorce, and he does not possess the power to forbid what is lawful. He only possesses the power to create the cause by which he forbids, which is divorce. This is not explicit in divorce, and it is not something for which the custom of the Law has been established regarding forbidding a wife, so the matter is unclear.

The fifth position: if he intended divorce by it, it is divorce; otherwise it is an oath. This is the view of Tawus, al-Zuhri, al-Shafiʿi, and a report from al-Hasan. The argument for this view is that it is implicit in divorce. If he intended it, it is divorce; if he did not intend it, it is an oath, because of the words of the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful for you?﴾ up to His words: ﴿the release of your oaths﴾.

The sixth position: if he intended three by it, it is three; if he intended one, it is one irrevocable divorce; if he intended an oath, it is an oath; and if he intended nothing, it is a lie with nothing in it. This was said by Sufyan, and al-Nakha'i related it from his companions. The argument for this view is that the wording allows for what he intended of these, so he follows his intention.

The seventh position: like this, except that if he intended nothing, it is an oath that he expiates. This is the view of al-Awza'i. The argument for this view is the apparent meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Allah has already ordained for you the release of your oaths﴾.

If he intended divorce by it, it is not an oath. If he divorced and did not intend divorce, it is an oath.

The eighth position: likewise, except that if he intended nothing, it is one irrevocable divorce, in application of the wording of forbidding.

The ninth position: that it carries the expiation of zihar. This is authentically transmitted from Ibn Abbas as well, and from Abu Qilabah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and Uthman al-Taymi. It is one of the reports from Imam Ahmad. The argument for this view is that Allah, exalted is He, made likening a woman to his mother, who is forbidden to him, a zihar, and called it a repugnant word and a falsehood. If likening her to a forbidden woman makes him a person who has done zihar, then when he explicitly declares her forbidden, it is even more fitting that it be zihar.

This is the most sound and well-grounded of the opinions, and it is supported by the fact that Allah did not grant the legally responsible person (al-mukallaf) the authority to make something forbidden (tahrim) or permissible (tahlil). That authority belongs to Allah the Exalted alone. He granted the servant only the actions and statements that bring about forbiddance or permissibility. So the cause (al-sabab) rests with the servant, and the ruling (hukm) rests with Allah the Exalted. If a man says, "You are to me like my mother's back" (anti 'alayya ka-zahri ummi), or says, "You are forbidden to me" (anti 'alayya haram), he has uttered an objectionable and false statement (al-munkar min al-qawl wa al-zur), and he has lied. Allah did not make her like his mother's back, nor did He make her forbidden to him. Yet by this statement, with its objectionable falsehood, He has obligated him to the more severe of the two expiations, which is the expiation of zihar (kaffarat al-zihar, a formal expiation for comparing one's wife to one's mother).

The tenth opinion: it is a single revocable divorce (talaqah wahidah). This is one of the two reports from Umar ibn al-Khattab, and it is the view of Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, the teacher of Abu Hanifa. The proof for this view is that a divorce by prohibition (talaq al-tahrim) does not necessarily imply a triple prohibition. It is satisfied by the least of it, and a single divorce is certain. So the wording is taken to mean that, because it is the certain meaning. This is analogous to prohibition by the completion of the waiting period ('iddah).

The eleventh opinion: he is held to what he intended by it regarding the basic fact of divorce and its number. If he intended prohibition without divorce, then it is an expiable oath (yamin mukaffirah). This is the view of al-Shafi'i. The proof for this view is that the wording is capable of all of these meanings, so none of them is fixed except by intention. If he intended mere prohibition, then it is a refusal to have her by means of prohibition, just as refusal by oath is, and she is not forbidden to him in either of the two cases.

The twelfth opinion: he is also held to his intention regarding the basic fact of divorce and its number. However, if he intended one divorce, it is a final irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in). If he did not intend divorce at all, then he is a mu'li (one who has made an oath of abstention, ila'). If he intended a lie, then it has no effect. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions. The proof for this view is that the wording admits of what has been mentioned. However, if he intended one divorce, it is irrevocable, because prohibition implies irrevocable separation (al-bayunah), which is of two kinds, minor (sughra) and major (kubra). The minor is the one that is definitely established, so it is taken into account rather than the major. There is another report from him: if he intended a lie, he is believed in matters between himself and Allah but is not accepted in legal judgment. Rather, he is a mu'li and not a zahir, according to him, whether he intended it or not. And if he explicitly said, "I mean by it zihar," he is not a zahir.

The thirteenth opinion: it is an oath, and what expiates an oath expiates it in every case. This was also reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn Abbas, Aisha, Zayd ibn Thabit, Ibn Mas'ud, Abdullah ibn Umar, Ikrimah, Ata, Makhul, Qatada, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Sulayman ibn Yasar, Jabir ibn Zayd, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Nafi', al-Awza'i, Abu Thawr, and others besides them. The proof for this view is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted mentioned the obligation of the dissolution of oaths (tahillat al-ayman) immediately after the prohibition of what is lawful. So it must certainly include this case. It is not permissible to make the dissolution of oaths apply to something other than what was mentioned before it, and the thing mentioned is removed from the ruling of dissolution, for which its mention was intended.

The fourteenth opinion: it is an aggravated oath (yamin mughallazah), in which the freeing of a slave (itq raqabah) is specifically required. This was also reported from Ibn Abbas, Abu Bakr, Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, and a group of the Successors (al-tabi'un). The proof for this view is that, since it is an aggravated oath, its expiation is made more severe by the requirement of freeing a slave with no alternative. The reason for its severity is that it includes the prohibition of what Allah has made lawful, which is not up to the servant. As for the statement of objectionable falsehood, if he intended it as a report, then it is a lie in his report and transgressive in his oath. So its expiation is made severe by the requirement of freeing a slave, just as the expiation of zihar is made severe by it, or by fasting two consecutive months, or by feeding sixty of the poor.

The fifteenth opinion: it is a divorce. Then, if she was not consummated, it is what he intended, a single divorce or more. If she was consummated, it is three divorces, even if he intended less. This is one of the two reports from Malik. The proof for this view is that since the wording implies prohibition, its ruling must follow from it. A woman who has not been consummated is forbidden by one divorce, while a woman who has been consummated is not forbidden except by three.

[The positions of the Malikis on the question]
After this, there are five opinions in the school of Malik. This one is the best known. The second is that it is three divorces in every case, whether he intended three or not. Abd al-Malik chose this in his al-Mabsut. The third is that it is a single irrevocable divorce absolutely. Ibn Khuwayz Mandad related this as a report from Malik. The fourth is that it is a single revocable divorce. This is the view of Abd al-Aziz ibn Abi Salamah. The fifth is that it is whatever he intended of that, absolutely, whether before consummation or after. You already know the justification for these opinions.

[The position of the Shafi'i school on the question]
As for the precise statement of the school of al-Shafi'i: if he intended zihar by it, it is zihar. If he intended prohibition by it, it is a prohibition which entails nothing except the obligation of expiation. If he intended divorce, it is divorce, and it is what he intended. If he stated it without specifying intention, his companions have three positions. The first is that it is explicit (sarih) in requiring expiation. The second is that nothing follows from it. The third is that for a slave-woman it is explicit in prohibition, which requires expiation, while for a free woman it is an allusion (kinayah). They said: the original verse was revealed concerning a slave-woman. They said: if a man says, "You are forbidden to me," and then says, "I intended by it zihar and divorce," Ibn al-Haddad said: he is told, "Specify one of the two matters, because a single word cannot be both zihar and divorce at once." It was also said: he is bound by whichever of the two he began with. They said: if a man claims a right against another man, and he denies it, and the claimant says, "The lawful is forbidden to you, the intention is my intention, not yours, I have nothing against you," and the other says, "The lawful is forbidden to me, and the intention in that is your intention, you have nothing from me," then the intention is the intention of the one swearing, not the one who makes him swear, because intention can only come from the one who has the authority to effect the ruling.

[Section: The position of Imam Ahmad on the question]
As for the precise statement of the position of Imam Ahmad: it is zihar in its very wording, even if he did not intend it, unless he intends divorce or oath by it, in which case he is held to what he intended. There is a second report from him that it is an oath in its very wording, unless he intends divorce or zihar by it, in which case he is held to what he intended. There is a third report from him that it is zihar in every case. If he intended divorce or oath by it, it is neither an oath nor a divorce, just as if he intended divorce or oath by saying, "You are to me like my mother's back," since both wordings are explicit in zihar. According to this third report, if he connects it with "I mean by it divorce," then is it divorce or zihar? There are two reports. The first is that it is zihar, just as if he said, "You are to me like my mother's back, I mean by it divorce or prohibition," since prohibition is explicit in zihar. The second is that it is divorce, because he has explicitly stated his intention with a word that admits of it, and at most it is an allusion in it. According to this report, if he says, "I mean by it one divorce," she is divorced once. If he says, "I mean by it the divorce," then is she divorced three times or once? There are two reports, whose basis is whether the obligation is taken as the genus or as the general. This is the precise statement and exposition of his position.

[The position of Ibn Taymiyyah on the question]
In this question there is another position beyond all of these, which is that if he pronounces prohibition, it is zihar even if he intended divorce by it. If he swears by it, it is an expiable oath. This is the choice of Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, and both the text and analogy indicate it. When he pronounces it, he has uttered an objectionable statement and falsehood, and he is more deserving of the expiation of zihar than one who compares his wife to a forbidden woman. When he swears by it, it is an oath among oaths, just as if he swore by pledging to free a slave, to perform the pilgrimage, or to give charity. This is pure analogy and understanding. Do you not see that if he says, "For Allah, I must free a slave, or perform the pilgrimage, or fast," it becomes binding on him? And if he says, "If I speak to so-and-so, then it is for Allah binding on me to do that," as an oath, it is an oath. Likewise, if he says, "He is a Jew or a Christian," he has disbelieved by that. And if he says, "If I do such-and-such, then he is a Jew or a Christian," it is an oath. The consistent extension of this, indeed its exact counterpart in every respect, is that if he says, "You are to me like my mother's back," it is zihar. So if he says, "If I do such-and-such, then you are to me like my mother's back," it is an oath. The consistent extension of this also is that if he says, "You are divorced," it is divorce, and if he says, "If I do such-and-such, then you are divorced," it is his oath. These are the sound principles, consistently applied, drawn from the Book, the Sunnah, and the balance of reason. And success is from Allah.

(Benefit)

Regarding the Almighty's words: ﴿Your two hearts have indeed inclined﴾

The Arabic language varies in how it uses the singular, dual and plural forms of a possessive noun (al-mudaf), according to the state of the noun it is attached to (al-mudaf ilayh).

If they attach a singular noun that is joined to a singular noun, they use the singular.

If they attach it to a collective noun (ism jam'), whether explicit or pronominal, they use the plural.

If they attach it to a dual noun, then the more correct usage in their language is the plural.

As in the Almighty's words: ﴿Your two hearts have indeed inclined﴾, although they are in fact two hearts; and as in His words: ﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾.

The Arabs also say: "Strike their necks" (اضرب أعناقهما), and this is the more eloquent in their usage.

(On the virtues of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him)
