ʿUmar saw, regarding the captives of Badr, that their necks should be struck, and the Qur'an came down in agreement with him. He saw that the wives of the Prophet ﷺ should be veiled, and the Qur'an came down in agreement with him.

He also saw that the Station of Ibrahim (Maqam Ibrahim) should be taken as a place of prayer, and the Qur'an came down in agreement with him.

And when the wives of the Prophet ﷺ gathered in jealousy against him, he said to them: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you, submitting (Muslim), believing (mu'minat)﴾, and the Qur'an came down in agreement with him.

"When ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy died, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up to pray over him. ʿUmar stood up and took hold of his garment and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, he is a hypocrite!' But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed over him, and Allah revealed to him: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, nor stand at his grave﴾ [al-Tawbah: 84]."

(Benefit)

Regarding the words of the Most High: ﴿thayyibat wa-abkaran﴾ (previously married and virgins).

It has been said that this is the "waw of eight" (wāw al-thamāniyah), because it comes after the seventh attribute; but this is not so.

The insertion of the waw here is necessary, because the attributes before it are intended to be combined in the women.

As for the two attributes of virginity and previous marriage, they cannot be combined, so the conjunction is required, since the intended meaning is that He will give him wives of both kinds: previously married and virgins.

(Section)
(From the notes of al-Qadi)
His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿They do not disobey Allah in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded﴾.
He said: The intended meaning is the command in this world, because in the Hereafter there is no command or prohibition upon the angels or anyone else, since worship has ceased.
In al-Bukhari, from Ali: "Today is action without reckoning, and tomorrow is reckoning without action."
I say: This is an error on his part, may Allah have mercy on him. Allah, the Exalted, commands the angels on the Day of Resurrection to seize the disbelievers and the criminals and drive them to the Fire and torment them therein. He commands His servants to prostrate to Him, so they fall down prostrating, except for the one whom Allah prevents from prostrating. He commands the believers, and they cross the Sirat. He commands the keepers of Paradise to open it for them, and the keepers of the Fire to open it for its people. He commands the angels of the heavens to descend to the earth. He commands concerning the whole matter of the Resurrection and what follows it. So the command on that Day belongs to Allah, and no one disobeys Allah on that Day even for the blink of an eye. His commands on that Day are for reward, punishment, and intercession for the angels, the prophets and others, governed by the power of the Creator.
So how can it be said that there is no command or prohibition in the Hereafter, such that it is said "they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and they do what they are commanded" refers only to this world?
Do you think that Allah, the Exalted, will not command them on the Day of Resurrection concerning the matter of the Fire, so that they do not disobey Him in it and do what they are commanded in it?
Yes, the Hereafter is not the abode of sowing, but it is the abode of harvest.
The commands and prohibitions of the Lord are established in both abodes, and likewise the commands of obligation are established in the barzakh and on the Day of Resurrection.
Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari related in his Maqalat from the People of the Sunnah that those to whom the call did not reach in this world will be held accountable on the Day of Resurrection.
So the statement of one who says: "The Hereafter is not an abode of obligation, command, or prohibition" is a false statement and a corrupt claim. And Allah is the Granter of success.
(Note)
Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah was asked: Which is better, the righteous among the children of Adam or the angels?
He answered: The righteous among mankind are better in terms of the perfection of the final outcome, and the angels are better in terms of the beginning.
For the angels now are in the Highest Companionship, purified from what the children of Adam are involved in, absorbed in the worship of the Lord. There is no doubt that these conditions now are more perfect than the conditions of mankind.
As for the Day of Resurrection after entry into Paradise, the state of the righteous among mankind becomes more perfect than the state of the angels.
With this distinction the secret of the preference becomes clear, the evidences of both groups agree, and each side is reconciled to its right. So the one who speaks on this subject must know the causes of excellence: first, their degrees and the relation of some of them to others, and the weighing between them; second, their relation to the one in whom they exist, in number and strength; third, consideration of their variation according to the variation of their locus.
For a quality may be a perfection for one person and not a perfection for another, rather the perfection of another lies in something else. Thus the perfection of Khalid ibn al-Walid lies in his bravery and wars, the perfection of Ibn Abbas in his jurisprudence and knowledge, and the perfection of Abu Dharr in his asceticism and detachment from the world.
These are four stations which the speaker is compelled to consider when discussing degrees of preference, and preferring types over types is easier than preferring individuals over individuals, and further from desire and bias.
Here is a subtle point that none perceives except one whom Allah has granted insight: that many who speak about preference sense their connection to and attachment to the one they prefer, even at a distance, and then begin to praise and exalt him. That connection and attachment stirs them to prefer and exaggerate, to enumerate the virtues of the preferred and overlook others, while their view of the one who is less preferred is the reverse.
Whoever examines the speech of most people on this subject finds that most of it is not free from this, and this contradicts the method of knowledge and justice which Allah accepts alone and does not approve anything else.
[Section: The disagreement of the jurists over designating one of the two parents for the girl's residence with him]
Here, effort (ijtihad) has been exerted concerning designating one of the two parents to be with the child and which of them is more suitable for her. Malik, Abu Hanifa, and Ahmad in one of his two reports designated the mother, and this is the sounder in evidence. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, in his well-known position, and the choice of most of his companions, designated the father.
Those who preferred the mother said: It is customary that the father deals with livelihood, going out, and meeting people, while the mother is secluded in her house. So the girl with her is undoubtedly safer and better protected, and her mother keeps watch over her constantly, unlike the father, who is in most times absent from the girl or in a situation resembling that. So placing her with her mother is safer and better for her.
They said: Every corruption that may arise with the mother arises with the father or more so, for if he leaves her alone in the house he cannot be secure about her, and if he leaves her with his wife or another, the mother is more compassionate toward her and more protective of her than a stranger.
They said: Furthermore, she needs to learn what is suitable for women of spinning and of caring for household affairs, and this is what women and not men undertake, so she is more in need of her mother to teach her what is fitting for a woman. Handing her over to her father would neglect this interest, and entrusting her to a foreign woman to teach her that, and her shuttling between the mother and him, and in that is training her to show herself and go out. So the interest of the girl, the mother, and the father is that she be with her mother. This is the view we do not choose other than.
Those who preferred the father said: Men are more jealous over daughters than women are, so a man's jealousy over his daughter is never equal to a mother's jealousy. How many a mother helps her daughter toward what she desires, being driven to it by the weakness of her mind, the speed with which she is deceived, and the weakness of the motive of jealousy in her nature, unlike the father. For this meaning and others, the Lawgiver made her marriage the affair of her father, not her mother, and did not give her mother any guardianship over her marriage at all, nor over her property. So it is one of the excellences of the Shari'ah that she be with her mother as long as she needs nurture and upbringing. But when she reaches a stage where she is desired and fit for men, then it is one of the excellences of the Shari'ah that she be with the one who is more jealous over her, more eager for her interest, and more protective of her than the mother.
They said: We see in the nature of the father and other men such jealousy, even with his immorality and wickedness, that it moves him to kill his daughter, sister, or ward if he sees from her what troubles him, because of the intensity of jealousy. And we see in the nature of women the opposite: looseness and easy deception. They said: This is the general rule for the two sexes, and no weight is given to what departs from the general rule. Furthermore, if we prefer one of the two parents, we must still observe his guarding and protecting of the child. For this reason Malik and al-Layth said: If the mother is not in a place of safekeeping and protection, or is not trustworthy, then the father may take the girl from her. Likewise Imam Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, in his well-known report, considers his capacity for protection and safeguarding. If he is negligent in this, or incapable of it, or not trustworthy, or a dayyuth (one who tolerates indecency in his household), while the mother is otherwise, then she is more entitled to the girl without doubt. Whoever we prefer by choice, by lot, or by himself, we prefer him only when the child's interest is achieved through him. If the mother is more protective than the father and more jealous than him, she is preferred over him, and there is no regard for a lot or for the child's choice in this situation, for he is weak in judgment, preferring idleness and play. If he chooses one who helps him toward that, his choice is not considered, and he is placed with the one who is more beneficial and better for him. The Shari'ah does not admit anything other than this. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Order them to pray at seven, strike them for it at ten, and separate them in their beds." And Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].
Al-Hasan said: Teach them, discipline them, and give them understanding of religion. So if the mother leaves him in the maktab and teaches him the Qur'an, but the child prefers play and the company of his peers, and his father permits him that, then the father is more entitled to him without choice or lot, and likewise the reverse. Whenever one of the two parents neglects the command of Allah and His Messenger concerning the child and leaves it, while the other attends to it, the latter is more entitled and more deserving of him.
I heard our Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, say: Two parents disputed over a child before one of the judges, and he gave the child the choice between them, and he chose his father. His mother said to him: Ask him why he chooses his father. So he asked him, and he said: My mother sends me every day to the kuttab, and the jurist beats me, while my father leaves me to play with the children. So he ruled that the child be given to the mother, and said: You are more entitled to him.
Our Shaykh said: When one of the two parents neglects teaching the child and the duty which Allah has imposed on him, he is sinful, and he has no guardianship over him. Rather, everyone who does not perform the obligation in his guardianship has no guardianship. Either his hand is removed from guardianship and someone who performs the obligation is appointed, or someone who performs the obligation with him is added to him, since the aim is obedience to Allah and His Messenger according to what is possible. Our Shaykh said: This right is not of the kind of inheritance which is obtained by kinship, marriage, or patronage, whether the heir is wicked or righteous. Rather this is of the kind of guardianship, which requires capacity for the obligation, knowledge of it, and performing it according to what is possible. He said: If it were supposed that the father married a woman who does not look after his daughter's interest and does not attend to her, while her mother is better at caring for her than that co-wife, then custody here is for the mother with certainty. He said: It should be known that the Lawgiver has no general text establishing preference of one of the two parents absolutely, nor giving the child choice between the two parents absolutely. The scholars agree that neither of them is determined absolutely; rather, the one who is aggressive and negligent is not preferred over the upright, just, and kind one. And Allah knows best.
[Section: The station of adab]
[Definition of adab]
Section: The station of adab
Among the stations of "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" is the station of adab.
Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].
Ibn Abbas and others said: Discipline them and teach them.
This word indicates gathering. Thus adab is the gathering of good qualities in the servant, and from it comes ma'dubah (a feast), which is the food around which people gather.
The science of adab is the science of correcting speech and address, hitting their proper targets, beautifying their wording, and guarding it against error and flaw.
It is a branch of general adab. And Allah knows best.
[Section: The kinds of adab]
Adab is of three kinds: adab with Allah, the Glorified; adab with His Messenger ﷺ and his Shari'ah; and adab with His creation.
Adab with Allah has three kinds:
The first: guarding one's dealings with Him from being mixed with deficiency.
The second: guarding one's heart from turning to other than Him.
The third: guarding one's will from attaching itself to what He detests.
Abu Ali al-Daqqaq said: The servant reaches Paradise through obedience to Allah, and reaches Allah through his adab in obedience.
He also said: I saw a man who wanted to stretch his hand during prayer to his nose, so he was restrained from his hand.
Ibn Ata said: Adab is standing with what is pleasing. It was said to him: What does it mean? He said: That you deal with Him, Glorified is He, with adab, secretly and openly. Then he recited:
"When she speaks she brings every charm, and when she is silent she brings every grace."
Abu Ali said: Whoever keeps company with kings without adab, ignorance leads him to death.
Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: When the knower abandons his adab with the One he knows, he has perished along with those who perish.
Abu Ali said: Abandoning adab necessitates expulsion. Whoever misbehaves on the carpet is returned to the door, and whoever misbehaves at the door is returned to tending the animals.
Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: Whoever disciplines himself with Allah's discipline becomes one of the people of Allah's love.
Ibn al-Mubarak said: We are in more need of a little adab than of much knowledge.
Al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him, was asked about the most beneficial adab. He said: Understanding of the religion, asceticism in this world, and knowledge of what is due to Allah from you.
Sahl said: The people sought help from Allah in fulfilling Allah's will, and they were patient for Allah in Allah's adab.
Ibn al-Mubarak said: We sought adab when those who disciplined us had passed away.
He also said: Adab for the knower is like repentance for the one who starts afresh.
Abu Hafs said, when al-Junayd said to him: "You have disciplined your companions with the adab of kings": Good adab outwardly is the sign of good adab inwardly. Adab with Allah is good companionship with Him, and performing outward and inward movements according to the requirements of glorification, reverence, and modesty, like the conduct of those who sit with and attend kings.
Abu Nasr al-Sarraj said: People in adab are of three classes.
As for the people of this world: their greatest adab is in eloquence and rhetoric, memorizing the sciences, the tales of kings, and the poetry of the Arabs.
As for the people of religion: their greatest adab is in purity of hearts, observing secrets, fulfilling covenants, guarding the moment, little attention to passing thoughts, good adab in the stations of seeking, the times of presence, and the ranks of nearness.

Sahl said: "Whoever subdues his self through adab worships God with sincerity."

Ibn al-Mubarak said: "People have said much about adab, but we say: it is knowing the self and its foolishness, and avoiding that foolishness."

Al-Shibli said: "Familiarity in speech with the Truth is abandoning adab."

Someone said: "The Truth, glory be to Him, says: Whoever I bind to standing with My names and attributes, I bind to adab; and whoever I unveil to the reality of My essence, I bind to ruin. So choose adab or ruin."

As evidence for this: when He, glory be to Him, unveiled Himself to the mountain, the mountain crumbled and was pulverized, and did not remain steadfast before the majesty of the Essence.

Abu Uthman said: "When love is sound, the lover is obliged to hold firmly to adab."

Al-Nuri, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Whoever does not show adab toward the moment, his moment is hatred."

Dhu al-Nun said: "When the seeker departs from the practice of adab, he returns from where he came."

Reflect on the states of the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, with Allah, and their address and their requests. How do you find them all filled with adab and upheld by it?

The Messiah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]

He did not say: "I did not say it."

There is a difference between the two answers in the reality of adab. Then he referred the matter to Allah's knowledge of the state and its secret, saying: ﴿You know what is in my self﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], then he disassociated himself from knowledge of the unseen of his Lord and what is specific to Him, saying ﴿And I do not know what is in Yourself﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116].

Then he praised his Lord and described Him as alone in knowing all the unseen. He said ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]. Then he denied that he had said to them anything other than what his Lord commanded him, which is pure tawhid, saying: ﴿I said to them only what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117].

Then he informed of his witness over them for the period of his stay among them, and that after his death he has no knowledge of them, and that Allah alone, Mighty and Majestic, is the One who, after death, has knowledge of them. He said: ﴿And I was a witness over them as long as I was among them; but when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117].

Then He described His witness, glory be to Him, as above every witness and more comprehensive. He said: ﴿And You are Witness over all things﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]. Then he said: ﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118]. This is among the most eloquent adab with Allah in such a station, meaning: it is the way of a master to show mercy to his servants and to be kind to them. These are Your servants; they are not servants of anyone else. So if You punish them, although they are Your servants, then unless they were the basest of wicked slaves, most rebellious against their master and most disobedient to him, You would not punish them. For the closeness of servanthood demands the master's kindness and mercy toward his servant. So why would the Most Merciful of the merciful, the Most Generous of the generous, and the Greatest of the benefactors punish His servants? Only because of their extreme defiance, their refusal to obey Him, and their full deserving of punishment.

The earlier statement ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116] has already been made, meaning: they are Your servants, and You know best their secrets and their open deeds. So if You punish them, You punish them with knowledge of what You punish them for. They are Your servants, and You know best what they committed and earned. Therefore there is in this no entreaty on their behalf, as the ignorant suppose, nor a surrender to bare will and dominion stripped of wisdom, as the Qadariyyah suppose.

Rather, it is an acknowledgment, confession, and praise of Him, glory be to Him, for His wisdom and justice, His perfect knowledge of their state, and their deserving of punishment.

Then he said: ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You are the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 118].

He did not say: "the Forgiving, the Merciful."

This is among the most eloquent adab with Allah, exalted is He. For he said it at a time of the Lord's anger against them and the command to send them to the Fire. So this is not a station of entreaty or intercession, but a station of disassociation from them. If he had said "indeed You are the Forgiving, the Merciful," it would have indicated an entreaty to his Lord on behalf of enemies against whom His anger was intense. So the station is one of agreement with the Lord in His anger toward those upon whom the Lord is angry. Thus he turned away from mentioning the two attributes by which one asks for His compassion, mercy, and forgiveness, to mentioning might and wisdom, which include perfect power and perfect knowledge.

The meaning is: if You forgive them, Your forgiveness is from perfect power and knowledge, not from inability to take vengeance against them, nor from ignorance on Your part of the measure of their crimes. This is because a created being may forgive another out of inability to take revenge on him, or out of ignorance of the measure of the offense against him. Perfection is the forgiveness of One who is both capable and all-knowing, and He is the Mighty, the Wise. Mentioning these two attributes in this station was exactly the adab in address.

In some reports: the bearers of the Throne are four. Two say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your forbearance after Your knowledge." And two say: "Glory be to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. To You be praise for Your pardon after Your power." For this reason each of these two attributes is paired with the other, as in His saying: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, Forbearing﴾ [an-Nisa': 12] and His saying: ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Pardoning and Competent﴾ [an-Nisa': 149].

Likewise is the saying of Abraham the Friend, peace be upon him: ﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me. And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink. And when I am ill, it is He who cures me﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 78–80]. He did not say: "and when He makes me ill," preserving adab with Allah.

Likewise is the saying of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, concerning the ship: ﴿So I intended to damage it﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].

He did not say: "So your Lord intended to damage it." Concerning the two boys he said: ﴿So your Lord intended that they reach their maturity﴾ [al-Kahf: 82].

Likewise is the saying of the believing jinn: ﴿And we do not know whether evil is intended for those on the earth, or whether their Lord intends for them guidance﴾ [al-Jinn: 10].

They did not say: "He intended it for them." Then they said: ﴿Or has their Lord intended for them right guidance?﴾ [al-Jinn: 10].

More subtle than this is the saying of Moses, peace be upon him: ﴿My Lord, indeed I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need﴾ [al-Qasas: 24].

He did not say: "feed me."

And the saying of Adam, peace be upon him: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. He did not say: "My Lord, You have empowered over me and decreed against me."

And the saying of Job, peace be upon him: ﴿Harm has touched me, and You are the Most Merciful of the merciful﴾ [al-Anbiya': 83]. He did not say: "so relieve me and heal me."

And the saying of Joseph to his father and brothers: ﴿This is the interpretation of my vision from before; my Lord has made it true. And He was certainly good to me when He took me out of prison﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. He did not say: "He took me out of the well," preserving adab with his brothers, and out of consideration for them, so as not to shame them by what happened in the well.

And he said ﴿and brought you from the desert﴾ [Yusuf: 100].

He did not say: "He removed from you the hardship of hunger and need," out of adab toward them. He attributed what happened to the cause and did not attribute it to the immediate agent, which is closer to him than the cause. He said: ﴿after Satan had caused discord between me and my brothers﴾ [Yusuf: 100]. Thus he gave generosity, nobility, and adab their due. For this reason the perfection of this disposition belongs only to the Messengers and Prophets, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them.

Of this kind is the Prophet's ﷺ command to a man that he cover his nakedness even when alone with no one watching, as adab with Allah, in proportion to nearness to Him, reverence and exaltation of Him, intense modesty before Him, and recognition of His dignity.

Some have said: Hold to adab outwardly and inwardly. No one who wrongs adab outwardly is punished except outwardly, and no one who wrongs adab inwardly is punished except inwardly.

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whoever neglects adab is punished by being deprived of the Sunan; whoever neglects the Sunan is punished by being deprived of the obligations; and whoever neglects the obligations is punished by being deprived of knowledge (ma'rifah).

It was said: Adab in action is a sign of the acceptance of the action.

The reality of adab is the practice of beautiful character. For this reason adab is the drawing out of the perfection that is in one's nature from potentiality into actuality.

Allah, glory be to Him, prepared man to receive perfection through the capacity and readiness He gave him, which He placed in him latent like fire in a flint. He inspired him, enabled him, made him know and guided him, sent His messengers to him, and sent down His books to him, to draw out that power by which He qualified him for his perfection into actuality. Allah, exalted, said: ﴿And a soul and He who proportioned it, and inspired it with its wickedness and its righteousness. He has certainly succeeded who purifies it, and he has certainly failed who corrupts it﴾ [ash-Shams: 7–10]. He expressed the disposition of the soul by proportioning it, to indicate balance and completeness.

Then He informed of its acceptance of both wickedness and righteousness, and that this was given to it as a test and trial. Then He singled out for success whoever purifies it, causing it to grow and elevating it, raising it by His adab with which He trained His messengers, prophets, and friends, which is piety. Then He decreed wretchedness upon whoever corrupts it, concealing it, belittling it, diminishing it, and suppressing it with wickedness. And Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, knows best.

[Section: Description of his ﷺ adab]

It is the custom of the people to mention at this point the saying of Allah, exalted, concerning His Prophet ﷺ when He showed him what He showed him: ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [an-Najm: 17].

Abu al-Qasim al-Qushayri opened the chapter on adab with this verse, as did others.

It seems they looked to the view of some of the exegetes who said: this is a description of his ﷺ adab in that station, since he did not turn to either side and did not go beyond what he saw. This is the perfection of adab. Its breach is for the observer to turn his gaze to his right or left, or to look beyond what is being observed. Turning aside is deviation, and looking beyond what is observed is transgression and overstepping. Thus the perfection of the observer's attention to what is observed is that he does not divert his sight to the right or left, nor exceed it.

This is the meaning I have gathered from Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul.

In this verse there are wondrous secrets, among the subtle aspects of adab befitting the most perfect of mankind ﷺ: his sight and his insight were in agreement there; they harmonized and confirmed each other regarding what his sight witnessed. Thus his insight was in accord with it, and what his insight witnessed was also a truth witnessed by the sight. So the witness of sight and insight were in agreement regarding him.

For this reason Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, said: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw. Will you then dispute with him about what he sees?﴾ [an-Najm: 11–12], meaning: the heart did not deny what he saw with his eyes.

For this reason Abu Ja'far recited it: ما كَذَّبَ الفُؤادُ ما رَأى with the letter dhal doubled, meaning the heart did not deny the sight, but confirmed it and agreed with it, due to the soundness of heart and sight, or the rectitude of insight and sight, and because what is seen by sight and insight is true. The majority recited ﴿ما كَذَبَ الفُؤادُ﴾ [an-Najm: 11] with the letter dhal light; it is transitive, and "what he saw" is its object: meaning his heart did not lie about what his eyes had seen, but agreed with it and concurred. Because his heart was in accord with his outward form, his outward with his inward, and his sight with his insight, the heart did not lie to the sight, and the sight did not exceed its limit so as to transgress, nor did it turn away from the seen so as to deviate; rather the sight remained balanced toward what was seen, neither exceeding it nor turning from it, just as the heart remained balanced in turning toward Allah and turning away from all else. He turned wholly toward Allah. The heart is susceptible to deviation and transgression, and both were absent from his heart and sight. His heart did not deviate by turning from Allah to other than Him, nor did it transgress by going beyond the station in which it was placed.

This is the utmost perfection and adab with Allah, to which none other can attain.

For the habit of souls, when placed in a lofty and elevated station, is to look toward what is higher than it and above it. Do you not see that Moses, peace be upon him, when he was placed in the station of speaking and intimate conversation, his soul sought the vision? But our Prophet ﷺ, when he was placed in that station, fulfilled its right fully, so why did neither his sight nor his heart turn to anything other than what he was placed in at all?

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 66, verse 6 (part 3 of 5):

Because of this, nothing obstructed him, and no desire could stop him, until he passed beyond the seven heavens, and he rebuked Musa (Moses) about it, his Lord. He said: "The Children of Israel say: 'I am the most honoured in character before Allah.' And this one has surpassed me and left me behind in ascent. Would that he were alone! But with him is his entire community." In the narration of al-Bukhari: "When I passed him, he wept. It was said to him: 'What makes you weep?' He said: 'I weep because a young man was sent after me, and more of his community will enter Paradise than of my community.'" Then he (ﷺ) surpassed him in ascent, and no will obstructed him, and no aspiration held him back from the perfection of servitude.

For this reason, his mount on his night journey would outpace his step, sight. It would set its foot at the limit of his gaze, in harmony with the state of its rider and the vastness of his distance, which outstripped the entire world in its journey. So the foot of the Buraq did not differ from the place of his sight, just as his foot (ﷺ) did not fall behind the place of his knowledge.

He (ﷺ) never ceased, in the depth of the perfection of his good manners with Allah, the Glorified, and in the completion of the ranks of his servitude to Him, until he tore through the veils of the heavens and passed beyond the seven layers, and passed beyond the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (Sidrat al-Muntaha), and reached a station of nearness that outdistanced the first and the last. There, the portions of nearness were poured upon him in full, and the clouds of the veils were dispersed from him, outwardly and inwardly, veil after veil. He was placed in a station that the prophets and messengers envied him for. And when he is in the Hereafter, he will be placed in a second station of nearness, which the first and the last will envy him for. And he stood firm there upon the straight path, out of the perfection of his good manners with Allah, his gaze neither swerved nor transgressed. Thus He established him in this world upon the most upright path of truth and guidance. He swore by His speech to this in the Wise Reminder, saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ya-Sin. By the Wise Qur'an. Indeed you are among the messengers, upon a straight path﴾ (Ya-Sin: 1-4). When the Day of Return comes, He will establish him upon the Sirat (bridge), asking for safety for his followers and the people of his Sunnah, until they cross it to the Gardens of Bliss. That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whomever He wills, and Allah is the possessor of tremendous bounty.

[Section: Good manners are the whole of religion]

Good manners (adab, i.e. refined conduct and courtesy) are the whole of religion. Covering the nakedness is part of good manners. Wudu' and ghusl from major impurity are part of good manners. Purifying oneself from filth is part of good manners, so that one stands before Allah pure. For this reason, they used to recommend that a man beautify himself in his prayer, for standing before his Lord.

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya (may Allah have mercy on him) say: Allah commanded a measure beyond covering the nakedness in prayer, which is taking adornment. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Take your adornment at every place of worship﴾ (al-A'raf: 31). So He tied the command to taking adornment, not to covering the nakedness, signalling that the servant should wear his finest and most beautiful clothes in prayer.

One of the early generation (al-salaf) owned a robe worth a great sum of money, and he would wear it at the time of prayer, saying: "My Lord is most deserving that I adorn myself for Him in my prayer."

It is known that Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, loves to see the effect of His blessing upon His servant, especially when he stands before Him. The best way to stand before Him is in one's garments and the blessing He has clothed him with, outwardly and inwardly.

And from good manners: the Prophet (ﷺ) forbade the one praying "to raise his gaze to the sky."

I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya (may Allah sanctify his soul) say: This is from the perfection of the good manners of prayer: that the servant should stand before his Lord with his head bowed, lowering his gaze to the ground, and not raising his sight upward.

He said: The Jahmiyya (a sect that denied Allah's attributes and His being above the heavens), when they did not understand this good manner, nor knew it, thought that this was evidence that Allah is not above His heavens on His Throne, as He has informed us about Himself. His messengers and all the people of the Sunnah agreed upon it.

He said: This is from their ignorance. Rather, this is evidence for whoever understood from the Messenger (ﷺ), contrary to their claim. For among the good manners with kings is that one who stands before them lowers himself toward the ground and does not raise his gaze to them. So what is the thought of the King of Kings, glorified is He?

I also heard him say, regarding his (ﷺ) prohibition of reciting the Qur'an in bowing and prostration: The Qur'an is the most noble speech, and it is the speech of Allah. The states of bowing and prostration are states of humility and lowliness on the part of the servant. So from good manners with the speech of Allah is that it should not be recited in these two states, and the state of standing and erectness is more appropriate for it.

And from good manners with Allah: one should not face His House or turn his back to it when relieving oneself, as was established from the Prophet (ﷺ) in the hadith of Abu Ayyub, Salman, Abu Hurayra, and others, may Allah be pleased with them. The correct view is that this good manner encompasses both open ground and buildings, as we have mentioned in another place.

And from good manners with Allah, in standing before Him in prayer: placing the right hand upon the left during the recitation. In the Muwatta' of Malik, from Sahl ibn Sa'd, it is said that this is from the Sunnah, and people used to be commanded with it. There is no doubt that it is from the good manners of standing before kings and great men. The Greatest of the Great is more deserving of it.

And among them: stillness in prayer. This is the constancy (dawam) about which Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 23).

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said, from Ibn Lahi'a: Yazid ibn Abi Habib narrated to me that Abu al-Khayr informed him, saying: We asked Uqba ibn Amir about the verse: ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 23). Are they the ones who pray continuously? He said: No. Rather, when he prays, he does not turn to his right, nor to his left, nor behind him.

I say: These are two matters: constancy in it (dawam), and persistence in it (mudawama). So this is constancy. And persistence is in His saying: ﴿And those who guard their prayers﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 34). Constancy has been explained as stillness of the limbs and tranquillity.

And from his good manners in listening to the recitation: that he should lend his hearing while being present (shahid).

And his good manners in bowing: that he should be upright, and magnify Allah, exalted is He, until there is nothing in his heart greater than Him, and he humbles and diminishes himself within his soul, until he becomes less than dust particles.

The point is that good manners with Allah, blessed and exalted is He, consist of upholding His religion and adopting His etiquette, outwardly and inwardly.

Good manners with Allah are never complete for anyone except through three things: knowledge of His names and attributes, knowledge of His religion and law, and of what He loves and what He dislikes; and a soul that is prepared, receptive, soft, and ready to accept the truth, in knowledge, action, and state. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

[Section: Good manners with the Messenger (ﷺ)]

As for good manners with the Messenger (ﷺ), the Qur'an is full of them.

The foremost of good manners with him is complete submission to him, and compliance with his command, and receiving his report with acceptance and affirmation, without burdening it with the opposition of false imagination, which one calls "rational," or with doubt or suspicion, or preferring over it the opinions of men and the refuse of their minds. Rather, one should single him out for judgment and submission, compliance and yielding, just as one singles out the Sender (Allah), the Glorified, for worship, humility, lowliness, turning in repentance, and reliance.

These are two monotheisms, and there is no salvation for the servant from the punishment of Allah except through both: the monotheism of the Sender, and the monotheism of following the Messenger.

So one should not seek judgment from anyone else, nor be content with the ruling of anyone else, nor should the execution of his command or the affirmation of his report be held back for presentation to the words of one's shaykh and imam, or the people of one's school and sect, or whomever one venerates.

If they permit it, he executes it and accepts his report. Otherwise, if he seeks safety, he turns away from his command and his report, and entrusts it to them. Otherwise, he distorts it from its proper places, and calls his distortion "interpretation" and "carrying." He says: "We interpret it and carry it to another meaning."

So for the servant to meet his Lord with every sin whatsoever, except associating partners with Allah, is better for him than to meet Him in this condition.

One day I addressed some of the eminent figures of these people, and I said to him: I ask you by Allah: if it were supposed that the Messenger (ﷺ) were alive among us, and he addressed us with his speech and his address, would it be an obligation upon us to follow him without presenting what he said to the opinion, speech, and school of others? Or should we not follow him until we present what we heard from him to the opinions and minds of people?

He said: Rather, the obligation would be to hasten to comply without turning to anything else.

I said: Then what abrogated this obligation for us? And by what was it abrogated?

He placed his finger upon his mouth, and remained stunned and bewildered, and did not utter a word.

This is the good manners of the elite with him: not opposing his command, nor associating partners with him, nor raising voices above his, nor disturbing the limbs with prayer and greetings upon him (ﷺ), nor detaching his speech from certainty, nor seeking from him knowledge of Allah or taking his rulings from him. Rather, in the matter of knowing Allah, reliance is placed on confused, bewildered, contradictory minds, and in rulings, on the imitation of men and their opinions. The Qur'an and the Sunnah are only recited by us for blessing, not because we receive from them the foundations of the religion or its branches. Whoever seeks that and aims at it, we shall oppose him and strive to cut off his roots and uproot his influence. ﴿Rather their hearts are in confusion about this, and they have deeds other than that which they are doing. Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, behold, they cry out. Do not cry out today; indeed, you will not be helped by Us. My verses were recited to you, but you used to turn back on your heels, arrogant, speaking nonsense at night, deserting. Have they not reflected upon the word, or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers? Or do they not recognise their Messenger, so they deny him? Or do they say, "He has madness"? Rather, he has brought them the truth, but most of them are averse to the truth. And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted. Rather, We have brought them their reminder, but they turn away from their reminder. Or do you ask them for payment? But the payment of your Lord is better, and He is the best of providers. And indeed you invite them to a straight path. And indeed those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path﴾ (al-Mu'minun: 63-74).

The one who advises himself and works for its salvation reflects upon these verses as they should be reflected upon, and contemplates them as they should be contemplated, and applies them to reality, and sees the wonder. He does not think they are restricted to a people who existed and then passed away. So the address is to you. Listen, O neighbour. And Allah is the One whose help is sought.

And from good manners with the Messenger (ﷺ): that one should not advance before him with a command, prohibition, permission, or disposal, until he himself commands, prohibits, or permits, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, do not put yourselves forward before Allah and His Messenger﴾ (al-Hujurat: 1). This remains until the Day of Resurrection and has not been abrogated. So advancing before his Sunnah after his death is like advancing before him during his life, and there is no difference between them for one of sound intellect.

Mujahid (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Do not presume over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Abu Ubayda said: The Arabs say: "Do not put yourself forward before the imam, nor before the father." That is, do not hasten with a command or prohibition without him.

Others said: Do not command until he commands, and do not forbid until he forbids.

And from good manners with him: that voices should not be raised above his voice. For this is a cause of the nullification of deeds. So what is the thought about raising opinions and the results of thoughts above his Sunnah and what he brought? Do you suppose that this would be a cause for the acceptance of deeds, while raising one's voice above his voice is a cause for their nullification?

And from good manners with him: that one should not make his call like the call of others. Allah said: ﴿Do not make the call of the Messenger among you like the call of some of you to others﴾ (al-Nur: 63). And regarding this, there are two opinions of the exegetes.

One of them: that you should not call him by his name, as some of you call others, but say: "O Messenger of Allah, O Prophet of Allah." According to this, the verbal noun is attributed to its object, meaning your calling of the Messenger.

The second: the meaning is: do not make his calling you equal to your calling one another. If he wishes he answers, and if he wishes he leaves it. Rather, when he calls you, there is no choice for you but to answer him, and it is not permissible for you to hold back from it at all. According to this, the verbal noun is attributed to its subject, meaning his calling you.

And from good manners with him: that when they are with him on a gathering matter, whether a sermon, a jihad, or garrison duty, none of them should go off to attend to his own need until he has sought his permission.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 66, verse 6 (part 4 of 5):

As Allah the Exalted says: ﴿The believers are only those who believe in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him on a matter of common concern, they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾ [al-Nur: 62]. If this is the conduct required in a matter restricted by a passing need, and they were not permitted to depart except with his permission, then how much more so with a path that is absolute in all the details of the religion, its foundations and its branches, its minute and its great matters? Is it lawful to go toward it without seeking his permission? ﴿So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know﴾ [al-Nahl: 43].

Among the courtesy owed to him is that his words should not be called into question; rather, opinions are to be questioned in light of his words. His text should not be opposed by analogy; rather, analogies are to be discarded and set aside in favour of his texts. His speech should not be distorted from its true meaning for the sake of a fancy that its adherents call "rational." Yes, it is (in their view) unknown and removed from correctness. The acceptance of what he (ﷺ) brought should not be made contingent upon the agreement of anyone. All of this stems from a lack of courtesy toward him (ﷺ), and it is pure audacity.

[Section: Courtesy with Creation]

As for courtesy toward creation: it is dealing with them, at their various ranks, in the manner that befits them. Each rank has its own courtesy. Toward parents there is a particular courtesy, and toward the father there is a courtesy specific to him that is more particular still. Toward the scholar there is another courtesy; toward the ruler there is a courtesy that befits him; and with his peers there is a courtesy that befits them. Toward strangers there is a courtesy other than his courtesy toward his companions and intimates. Toward a guest there is a courtesy other than his courtesy toward the members of his household.

For every state there is a courtesy: there are courtesies for eating, for drinking, for riding, for entering, for leaving, for travelling, for residing, and for sleeping. There are courtesies for urinating, for speaking, and for silence and listening.

A person's courtesy is the sign of his happiness and success, and a lack of courtesy is the sign of his wretchedness and ruin. Thus the good of this world and the Hereafter has been attracted by nothing like courtesy, and their deprivation has been brought about by nothing like a lack of courtesy.

Consider courtesy toward parents: how it saved its possessor from the confinement of the cave when the rock sealed them in? And neglecting it toward the mother, through (misinterpretation) and devoting oneself to prayer, how his companion was tested by the destruction of his hermitage, by people striking him, and by their accusing him of immorality?

Reflect on the states of every wretched, deluded and turning-away person: how you will find that a lack of courtesy is what drove him to deprivation?

Consider the lack of courtesy of ʿAwf toward Khalid: how it deprived him of the spoils after he had been struck down by his hands?

And consider the courtesy of the Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, toward the Prophet ﷺ in prayer, that he should not go forward before him. He said: "It was not fitting for the son of Abu Quhafa to go forward before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ." How his stature was inherited by him, and leadership of the community after him! So that retreat behind him, while he (ﷺ) had signalled to him to remain in his place, was a bound and a striving forward: for every step backward were stages forward, in which the necks of the mounts are cut.  And Allah knows best.

[Section: The Reality of Courtesy]

The author of "al-Manazil" said:

Courtesy is: keeping the limit between excess and neglect, by knowing the harm of transgression.

This is among the finest definitions. Deviation to either extreme of excess or neglect is a lack of courtesy. Courtesy is standing in the middle between the two extremes, so that one does not fall short of the limits of the Sharia in completing them, nor exceed what they were set as limits for. Both are transgression, and Allah does not love transgressors. And transgression is bad courtesy.

Some of the early generations said: "The religion of Allah lies between the one who exaggerates in it and the one who turns away from it."

Losing courtesy through neglect is like one who does not complete the members of wudu, and does not perform the prayer with the courtesies that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prescribed and practised. These are close to a hundred courtesies, between obligatory and recommended.

Losing it through excess is like whispering in forming the intention, raising the voice with it, loudly reciting the remembrances and supplications which were prescribed to be silent, and lengthening what the Sunna intends to shorten or omit, such as the first tashahhud and the salam, whose omission is a Sunna; and exceeding in length beyond what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did, not in accordance with what the thieves of prayer and those who peck at it imagine and desire. For the Prophet ﷺ would not command a matter and then contradict it, and Allah protected him from that. He used to command them to be brief, and led them with the longer surahs (al-Saffat); he commanded them to be brief when the noon prayer was established, and a man would go to al-Baqi', attend to his need, return to his family, perform wudu, and catch the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the first rak'a. This is the brevity he commanded, not the pecking and stealing of prayer. For that is abbreviation; rather, it is limiting oneself to what the name applies to, and by which one is called a worshipper, like the eating of one in dire hunger who takes what keeps his life; would that he were satisfied according to the other opinion. It is like a hungry man presented with a very delicious meal, who takes a morsel or two: what do they avail him? But if he felt his hunger, he would not rise from the food until he was satisfied with it, and he is able to do so. But the heart is satisfied with something else.

An example of this moderation regarding the rights of the prophets, peace be upon them: that one should not exaggerate about them as the Christians exaggerated about the Messiah, nor turn away from them as the Jews did. The Christians worshipped them; the Jews killed them and denied them. The middle nation believed in them, honoured them, supported them, and followed what they brought.

An example of this in the rights of creation: one should not neglect fulfilling their rights, nor be so absorbed in them that one is occupied with them to the detriment of the rights of Allah, or of completing them, or of the good of one's religion and heart; and one should not turn away from them until one wholly abandons them. For both extremes are harmful transgression. On this definition, the reality of courtesy is justice. And Allah knows best.

[Section: On the obligation to discipline and teach children, and to be just among them]

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].

ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Teach them and discipline them." Al-Hasan said: "Command them to obey Allah, and teach them good." In the Musnad and the Sunan of Abu Dawud, from the hadith of ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Command your children to pray at seven, and strike them for it at ten, and separate them in their beds." In this hadith there are three courtesies: he commanded them, struck them for it, and separated them in their beds.

Al-Hakim narrated from Abu al-Nadr al-Faqih: Muhammad ibn Hamawiyya narrated to us, his father narrated to us, al-Nadr ibn Muhammad narrated to us, from al-Thawri, from Ibrahim ibn Muhajir, from ʿIkrima, from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "Open for your children the first word as 'There is no god but Allah,' and prompt them at death with 'There is no god but Allah.'"

In the History of al-Bukhari, through the narration of Bishr ibn Yusuf, from ʿAmir ibn Abi ʿAmir, who heard Ayyub ibn Musa al-Qurashi, from his father, from his grandfather, from the Prophet ﷺ who said: "No parent has bestowed upon a child a better gift than good discipline." Al-Bukhari said: "His grandfather's hearing from the Prophet ﷺ is not sound."

In the Mu'jam of al-Tabarani, from the hadith of Simak, from Jabir ibn Samura, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "For one of you to discipline his child is better for him than that he give a sadaqa of half a sa' every day to the poor."

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned, from the hadith of Muhammad ibn al-Fadl ibn ʿAtiyya, who is weak, from his father, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They said: "O Messenger of Allah, we know what the right of the father is; what is the right of the child?" He said: "That he make his name good and make his discipline good." Sufyan al-Thawri said: "A man should compel his child to seek hadith, for he will be questioned about it." He also said: "This hadith is precious: whoever seeks through it this world finds it, and whoever seeks through it the Hereafter finds it." ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar said: "Discipline your son, for you will be questioned about him: what did you discipline him in, and what did you teach him? And he will be questioned about his dutifulness and obedience to you."

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned, from the hadith of Muslim ibn Ibrahim: Shaddad ibn Saʿid narrated to us, from al-Jurayri, from Abu Saʿid and Ibn ʿAbbas, who both said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
"Whoever has a child born to him, let him make his name good and his discipline good. When he reaches maturity, let him marry him off. If he reaches maturity and he is not married and commits a sin, then its sin is upon his father."

Sa'id ibn Mansur said: Hazm narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Hasan, and Kathir ibn Ziyad asked him about the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and offspring comfort to our eyes﴾ [al-Furqan: 74]. He said: "O Abu Saʿid, what is this comfort of the eyes? Is it in this world or in the Hereafter?" He said: "No, by Allah, it is in this world." He said: "And what is it?" He said: "By Allah, that Allah shows the servant from his wife, from his brother, from his intimate, obedience to Allah. No, by Allah, there is nothing more beloved to the Muslim than to see a child, or a parent, or an intimate, or a brother, obedient to Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

Al-Bukhari narrated in his Sahih, from the hadith of Nafi', from Ibn ʿUmar, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
"Each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock. The ruler is a shepherd over the people and is responsible for his flock; the man is a shepherd over his household and is responsible for them; the woman is a shepherdess over her husband's house and children and is responsible for them; the servant is a shepherd over his master's property and is responsible for it. Truly, each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock."

(Section)

Among the rights of children is justice between them in giving and withholding.

In the Sunan, the Musnad of Ahmad, and the Sahih of Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:
"Be just between your children; be just between your children."

In Sahih Muslim:
"The wife of Bashir said to him: 'Gift my son a slave, and have the Messenger of Allah ﷺ bear witness for me.' So he came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: 'The daughter of so-and-so asked me to gift her son my slave.'
He said to him: 'Does he have brothers?' He said: 'Yes.'
He said: 'Have you given each of them the like of what you have given him?'
He said: 'No.'
He said: 'This is not fitting, and I will not bear witness except to what is right.'"

Imam Ahmad narrated it and said in it: "Do not make me a witness to injustice. Your sons have a right over you: that you be just between them."

In the Two Sahihs, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, that his father brought him to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "I have gifted this son of mine a slave that I had." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Have you given all your children the like of this?" He said: "No." He said: "Return it."

In a narration of Muslim: "He said: 'Have you done this to all your children?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Fear Allah and be just among your children.' So my father retracted that charity."

In the Sahih: "Bear witness to this other than me." This is a command of warning, not of permission, for that gift was injustice by the explicit text of the hadith, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ does not permit anyone to bear witness to the validity of injustice.

Who, then, was going to bear witness to that gift, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused to bear witness to it, and informed that it was not valid, that it was injustice, and that it was contrary to justice?

It is strange that his saying "be just among your children" should be taken to mean other than obligation, when it is an absolute command emphasised three times, and the one commanding has informed that its opposite is injustice, that it is not valid, that it is not right, and that after the truth there is nothing but falsehood.

Moreover, justice is obligatory in every state. Had the command to it been absolute, it would still have to be read as obligation; how much more so when ten things accompany it that emphasise its obligation, as you may consider in the wording of the story.

Al-Bayhaqi mentioned, from the hadith of Abu Ahmad ibn ʿAdi: al-Qasim ibn Mahdi narrated to us, Yaʿqub ibn Kasib narrated to us, ʿAbd Allah ibn Muʿadh narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from al-Zuhri, from Anas:
"A man was sitting with the Prophet ﷺ, and his son came and he kissed him and seated him on his lap. Then his daughter came and he took her and seated her beside him. The Prophet ﷺ said: 'Then you have not been just between them.'"

The early generations used to recommend being just among children in kissing.

Some scholars said: Allah, glory be to Him, will question the father about his child on the Day of Resurrection before He questions the child about his father. For just as the father has a right over his son, the son has a right over his father. As Allah said: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man kindness to his parents﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 8].

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said: "Teach them and discipline them." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and be good to parents and to the near of kin﴾ [al-Nisa': 36]. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Be just among your children."

So Allah's charge to fathers regarding their children precedes the charge to children regarding their fathers. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And do not kill your children out of fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31].

Whoever neglects teaching his child what benefits him, and leaves him unguided, has done him the utmost harm. Most of children's corruption comes from their fathers, through neglect of them and failure to teach them the obligations and Sunnas of the religion; they lose them while young, so they do not benefit themselves, and they do not benefit their fathers when grown. As one of them reproached his son for disobedience, saying: "O father, you disobeyed me when I was small, so I disobeyed you when you were old; you neglected me as an infant, so I neglected you in old age."

(Useful sections on raising children, whose outcomes are praised in later life)

(Section)

It is fitting that a newborn be nursed by someone other than his mother after birth for two or three days, which is the better course, because her milk at that time is thick and mixed with humours, unlike the milk of one who has settled into nursing. All the Arabs take care in this, so that they send their children to be nursed by women of the desert, as the Prophet ﷺ was nursed among the Banu Sa'd.

(Section)

It is fitting that children not be carried and paraded about until three months or more have passed, because of their recent emergence from their mothers' wombs and the weakness of their bodies.

(Section)

It is fitting that they be restricted to milk alone until their teeth come through, for the weakness of their stomachs and the weakness of their digestive power for food. When their teeth come through, their stomachs grow strong and they are nourished by food. Allah, glory be to Him, delayed their emergence until the time of their need for food, out of His wisdom, gentleness, and mercy toward the mother and her nipple, so that the child does not bite her with his teeth.

(Section)

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 66, verse 6 (part 5 of 5):

It is fitting to introduce them gradually to food. The first food they are given should be soft: they are fed bread soaked in hot water, and milk and fresh milk (ḥalīb). After that, they are given cooked dishes and broths (amrāq) that are free of meat. After that, they are given very finely prepared meat, after it has been thoroughly chewed or crushed into a smooth paste.

(Section)

When they approach the time of speech and it is desired to make speaking easier for them, their tongues should be rubbed with honey and Andarani salt (a salt named after Andaran), because of their clearing effect on the heavy humours that prevent speech. When the time for them to speak comes, they should be taught: "There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." The first thing to reach their hearing should be the knowledge of Allah, glorified is He, and His oneness, and that He, glorified is He, is above His Throne, watching them, hearing their speech, and with them wherever they are. The Children of Israel often named their children "Immanuel," and the meaning of this word is "Our God is with us." For this reason, the most beloved names to Allah are ʿAbd Allah and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, so that when the child is aware and understands, he knows that he is the servant of Allah and that Allah is his master and lord.

(Section)

When the time for teething arrives, it is fitting to rub their gums every day with butter and clarified butter (samn), and to massage the vertebrae of the neck (khuraz al-ʿunuq) thoroughly. They should be guarded with the utmost care during teething, until the teeth have fully formed and gained strength, and they should be completely prevented from hard things, because allowing access to them exposes the teeth to decay, crookedness and defects.

(Section)

The parents should not be distressed by the child's crying and screaming, especially when he cries for milk because he is hungry, for he benefits greatly from that crying. It exercises his limbs, widens his intestines, opens his chest, warms his brain, protects his temperament, stirs up his innate heat, moves his nature to expel its excesses, and expels the brain's secretions of mucus and other matter.

(Section)

The swaddling and binding should not be neglected, even if it is hard on him, until his body becomes firm, his limbs strong, and he sits on the ground. Then he should be exercised and trained in movement and standing, little by little, until it becomes a faculty and strength for him, and he does it on his own.

(Section)

The child should be protected from everything that frightens him: harsh, dreadful sounds, hideous sights, and disturbing movements, for these may corrupt his rational faculty by weakening it, so that he does not benefit from it when he grows up. If something of this kind befalls him, one should hasten to remedy it with its opposite, to soothe him with something that makes him forget it, to put the breast to his mouth immediately and hurry to nurse him so that the disturbing thing leaves him and is not imprinted on his retentive faculty, which would make it hard to remove. Gentle rocking should be used until he sleeps and forgets. This matter should not be neglected, for neglecting it leaves fear and terror settled in his heart. He grows up with it, and it becomes difficult and nearly impossible to remove.

(Section)

The condition of the newborn changes when his teeth come in; vomiting, fevers and bad temper are provoked, especially if teething happens in winter and cold, or in summer and intense heat. The best times for teething are spring and autumn. The time of teething is at seven months, though it may come at five and may be delayed until ten. So one should handle his care during teething gently, bring him to the bathhouse repeatedly, and feed him light food so that his stomach is not overfilled. Diarrhoea may occur, so his belly should be bound with what suffices, such as a woollen band with fine cumin, celery and anise on it, and his gums rubbed with what was mentioned earlier. Yet diarrhoea at that time is better for him than constipation. If his bowels are constipated during teething, one should hasten to loosen his nature, for nothing harms a child during teething more than constipation, and nothing benefits him more than gentle, regular ease. The most suitable thing for loosening is cooked honey from which suppositories (fatāʾil) are made and inserted, or ground basil mixed with honey from which suppositories are likewise made. The nursing mother should lighten her food and drink at that time and avoid harmful foods.

(Section)

Among the things to be guarded against is making the child walk before his time, for this causes his legs to twist and bend because of their weakness and their susceptibility to that. Be extremely careful not to withhold from him what he needs: vomiting, sleep, food, drink, sneezing, urination, or the letting out of blood, for withholding these has bad consequences for both the child and the adult.

(Section)

What the child needs most urgently is attention to his character, for he grows up upon what his educator habituates him to in childhood: spite, anger, obstinacy, haste, levity in following his desires, frivolity, stubbornness and greed. Later it becomes difficult to remedy this, and these traits become firm qualities and settled dispositions in him. Even if one guards him in the utmost way, they will expose him sooner or later. This is why you find most people's characters twisted, owing to the upbringing they grew up with. Likewise, when the boy comes to understand, he must be kept away from gatherings of idle play, falsehood, singing, hearing obscenity, innovations and evil talk, for once these cling to his hearing, it becomes hard for him to part with them when he is grown, and hard for his guardian to rescue him from them. Changing habits is among the most difficult matters; it requires its owner to acquire a second nature, and leaving the rule of one's nature is exceedingly difficult.

His guardian should keep him as far as possible from taking from others, for once he becomes accustomed to taking, it becomes his nature, and he grows up taking rather than giving. He should be accustomed to giving and bestowing, and when the guardian wishes to give something, he should give it through the child's hand so that he tastes the sweetness of giving. He should be kept from lying and betrayal even more than from deadly poison, for once the path of lying and betrayal is made easy for him, it spoils for him the happiness of this world and the Hereafter, and deprives him of every good.

He should be kept from laziness, idleness, ease and comfort; rather, he should be trained in their opposites, and not allowed rest except in what gathers his soul and body for work. Laziness and idleness have bad consequences and regrettable ends, while diligence and toil have praiseworthy consequences, either in this world, or in the next, or in both. So the most restful people are the most toilsome, and the most toilsome are the most restful. Leadership in this world and happiness in the Hereafter are reached only over a bridge of toil. Yaḥyā ibn Abī Kathīr said: "Knowledge is not attained through physical comfort." He should be accustomed to waking at the end of the night, for that is the time of dividing spoils and distributing prizes: some are given little, some much, and some are deprived. When he becomes accustomed to this in childhood, it becomes easy for him when he is grown.

He should be kept from excess in food, speech and sleep, and from mixing too much with people, for the loss lies in these excesses, which cost the servant the good of his worldly life and his Hereafter. He should be kept, as far as possible, from the harms of desires connected to the belly and the private parts. Allowing him access to their means and granting him latitude in them corrupts him to a degree that makes his later reform difficult. How many have made their children, the fruit of their hearts, wretched in this world and the Hereafter by neglecting them, failing to discipline them, and helping them to satisfy their desires, while thinking they are honouring them when they are humiliating them, and that they are showing mercy when they are wronging and depriving them. Thus the father loses the benefit of his child, and the child's share of this world and the next is lost. If you consider the corruption of children, you will find that most of it comes from the fathers.

(Section)

One must be utterly vigilant against allowing him to consume anything that removes reason, whether an intoxicant or otherwise; against letting him keep company with someone whose corruption is feared, or with his talk; and against letting him take things into his hand, for all of that is ruin. Once it is made easy for him, one has made dayyātha (complicity in the dishonour of one's family) easy, and a dayyūth will not enter Paradise. Nothing corrupts children like the heedlessness and neglect of parents, and their treating sparks among clothes as trivial. Most parents rely upon their children in the same way that the most fiercely hostile enemy relies upon his enemy, while they are unaware. How many a father has deprived his child of the good of this world and the Hereafter, and exposed him to ruin in both! All of this is the consequence of parents' neglect of Allah's rights and their failure to fulfil them, and their turning away from what Allah has made obligatory upon them of beneficial knowledge and righteous action. That deprives them of benefit from their children, and deprives the children of their goodness and their benefit to them. This is among the punishments of parents.

(Section)

He should be kept from wearing silk, for it corrupts him and makes him effeminate by nature, just as sodomy effeminizes, and likewise wine-drinking, theft and lying. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Silk and gold are forbidden to the males of my community and permitted to their females." Even if the child is not legally responsible, his guardian is responsible, and it is not permitted for him to allow him to do what is forbidden, for he will become accustomed to it, and weaning him from it will be difficult. This is the more sound of the two opinions of the scholars. Those who did not consider it forbidden for him argued that he is not legally responsible, so his wearing silk is not forbidden, like an animal. This is among the most corrupt analogies, for although the child is not responsible, he is prepared for responsibility. That is why he is not allowed to pray without ablution, or to pray naked and impure, or to drink wine, gamble or commit sodomy.

(Section)

Among the things that should be considered is the child's condition, and what he is disposed and prepared for among actions. One should know that he was created for certain things, and not compel him toward something else in cases where that is permitted by the Sharia. If he is compelled toward what he is not disposed to, he will not prosper in it and will miss what he was prepared for. If you find him of good understanding, sound comprehension, good memory and attentiveness, these are signs of his readiness and aptitude for knowledge, so inscribe it on the tablet of his heart while it is still empty, for it will take firm root in him, remain, and grow with him. If you find him otherwise in every respect, disposed to horsemanship and its means, such as riding, archery and playing with the lance, and that he has no aptitude for knowledge and was not created for it, then enable him to acquire the means of horsemanship and to train in them, for that is more beneficial for him and for the Muslims. If you find him otherwise, not created for that, and you see his eye open to some craft, disposed and receptive to it, a permissible craft beneficial to people, then enable him to pursue it. All of this should come after teaching him what he needs for his religion, for that is easy for everyone, so that Allah's proof may be established against the servant, for He has the conclusive proof against His servants, just as He has the abundant blessing upon them. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 66, verse 8:

[Section: Sincere Repentance (al-tawbah al-nasuh)]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾.

He made the protection from the evil of misdeeds, which is their expiation, and the entry into the gardens, which is the attainment of what the servant loves, contingent upon the attainment of sincere repentance (al-tawbah al-nasuh). The word nasuh is in the form fa'ul, which is used in place of fa'il for the purpose of emphasis, as in shakur (very grateful) and sabur (very patient). The root n-s-h (ن ص ح) originally means the purification of a thing from adulteration and foreign impurities, and it coincides in the greater derivation (al-ishtiqaq al-akbar) with nasaha, meaning "became pure." Thus, sincerity (al-nush) in repentance, worship and counsel means purifying them from every adulteration, deficiency and corruption, and performing them in the most complete manner. Al-nush is the opposite of deceit (al-ghish).

The expressions of the early scholars (al-salaf) about it differ, but they all return to one thing. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: Sincere repentance is that one repents from the sin and then does not return to it, just as milk does not return to the udder. Al-Hasan al-Basri said: It is that the servant is remorseful for what has passed, resolved not to return to it. Al-Kalbi said: It is that he seeks forgiveness with the tongue, feels remorse in the heart, and refrains with the body. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab said: "A sincere repentance, by which you counsel your own souls." He took it to mean counselling (nasihah) for the one who repents, like darub (one who strikes much) as the form derived from darib (one who strikes).

Those who hold the first view take it to mean the passive (bi-ma'na al-maf'ul), i.e., the penitent has been sincere in it and it has not been mixed with deceit. It is either in the sense of "sincerely performed" (manṣuh fiha), like rakubah (a ridden animal) and halubah (a milked animal), meaning marku bah (ridden) and mahlub ah (milked), or in the sense of the active participle, i.e., "sincere," like khalisah (pure) and sadiqah (truthful).

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi said: It comprises four things: seeking forgiveness with the tongue, ceasing with the body, resolving with the heart not to return, and abandoning bad companions.

I say: Sincerity in repentance includes three things:

The first: generalising all the sins and encompassing them in the repentance, such that it leaves out no sin without including it.

The second: the gathering of resolve and truthfulness in their entirety upon it, such that no hesitation, wavering or waiting remains in him, but he gathers all his will and determination upon it, hastening to it.

The third: purifying it from the impurities and causes that taint its sincerity, and that it occurs purely out of fear of Allah and awe of Him, and desire for what is with Him, and dread of what is with Him, not like one who repents to preserve his status and dignity, his position and leadership, or to preserve his condition, or to preserve his strength and wealth, or to seek people's praise, or to flee their blame, or lest foolish people dominate him, or to satisfy his worldly appetite, or because he has become bankrupt and incapable, and similar causes that taint its validity and its purity for Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The first relates to what one repents from, the third relates to whom one repents to, and the middle relates to the penitent's own self and soul. So the counsel of repentance is truthfulness in it, sincerity, and generalising the sins by it. There is no doubt that this repentance necessarily entails seeking forgiveness and includes it, erases all sins, and is the most complete form of repentance. And Allah is the One whose help is sought, and upon Him is reliance, and there is no power nor strength except with Allah.

(Section)
